NMF strikes a balance between PCA and K-Means for concept extraction, offering good reconstruction, sparsity, stability, and in-distribution reconstructions.
The last layer is preferable for both concept extraction and concept importance estimation.
For concept importance in the penultimate layer, Gradient Input, Integrated Gradients, Occlusion, and RISE are optimal for faithfulness metrics (C-Deletion, C-Insertion, C-µFidelity).
The strategic cluster graph visualizes the main classification strategies used by a model and helps explain misclassifications.
The framework enables the derivation of new concept importance methods and their evaluation using adapted faithfulness metrics.
papers.abstract: In recent years, concept-based approaches have emerged as some of the most promising explainability methods to help us interpret the decisions of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). These methods seek to discover intelligible visual 'concepts' buried within the complex patterns of ANN activations in two key steps: (1) concept extraction followed by (2) importance estimation. While these two steps are shared across methods, they all differ in their specific implementations. Here, we introduce a unifying theoretical framework that comprehensively defines and clarifies these two steps. This framework offers several advantages as it allows us: (i) to propose new evaluation metrics for comparing different concept extraction approaches; (ii) to leverage modern attribution methods and evaluation metrics to extend and systematically evaluate state-of-the-art concept-based approaches and importance estimation techniques; (iii) to derive theoretical guarantees regarding the optimality of such methods. We further leverage our framework to try to tackle a crucial question in explainability: how to efficiently identify clusters of data points that are classified based on a similar shared strategy. To illustrate these findings and to highlight the main strategies of a model, we introduce a visual representation called the strategic cluster graph. Finally, we present https://serre-lab.github.io/Lens, a dedicated website that offers a complete compilation of these visualizations for all classes of the ImageNet dataset.

papers.title: ENNGene: an Easy Neural Network model building tool for Genomics
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents ENNGene, a user-friendly tool with a graphical interface that simplifies the process of building, training, and interpreting deep learning models for genomics data.
papers.conclusion: ENNGene empowers genomics researchers to use deep learning for their data and will be an important tool for the genomics research community.
papers.key_findings:
ENNGene models achieve state-of-the-art performance on the RBP24 dataset, with an average AUROC of 0.947.
Including evolutionary conservation as an input branch improves performance for most proteins in the RBP24 dataset.
The tool provides interpretability through Integrated Gradients, highlighting important input positions.
papers.limitation: The tool currently requires manual tuning of hyperparameters and architecture selection, which could be automated in the future.
future_direction: Incorporating Neural Architecture Search (NAS) for automatic architecture optimization.
Adding a module for automated hyperparameter tuning.
Setting up a dedicated server with common genome references to simplify data input.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The recent big data revolution in Genomics, coupled with the emergence of Deep Learning as a set of powerful machine learning methods, has shifted the standard practices of machine learning for Genomics. Even though Deep Learning methods such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are becoming widespread in Genomics, developing and training such models is outside the ability of most researchers in the field. Results Here we present ENNGene - Easy Neural Network model building tool for Genomics. This tool simplifies training of custom CNN or hybrid CNN-RNN models on genomic data via an easy-to-use Graphical User Interface. ENNGene allows multiple input branches, including sequence, evolutionary conservation, and secondary structure, and performs all the necessary preprocessing steps, allowing simple input such as genomic coordinates. The network architecture is selected and fully customized by the user, from the number and types of the layers to each layer's precise set-up. ENNGene then deals with all steps of training and evaluation of the model, exporting valuable metrics such as multi-class ROC and precision-recall curve plots or TensorBoard log files. To facilitate interpretation of the predicted results, we deploy Integrated Gradients, providing the user with a graphical representation of an attribution level of each input position. To showcase the usage of ENNGene, we train multiple models on the RBP24 dataset, quickly reaching the state of the art while improving the performance on more than half of the proteins by including the evolutionary conservation score and tuning the network per protein. Conclusions As the role of DL in big data analysis in the near future is indisputable, it is important to make it available for a broader range of researchers. We believe that an easy-to-use tool such as ENNGene can allow Genomics researchers without a background in Computational Sciences to harness the power of DL to gain better insights into and extract important information from the large amounts of data available in the field. Contact panagiotis.alexiou@ceitec.muni.cz

papers.title: From Parameters to Performance: A Data-Driven Study on LLM Structure and Development
papers.research_question: How do structural configurations of large language models (LLMs) affect their performance across different benchmarks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a large-scale dataset of LLM structural configurations and performance, and provides data-driven insights into how specific structural parameters (like layer depth and FFN size) affect performance across different task types, validated through mechanistic interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: Structural parameters of LLMs have distinct and quantifiable impacts on different task types, and data-driven analysis combined with mechanistic interpretability can provide actionable insights for model optimization and design.
papers.key_findings:
Layer depth is the most influential structural factor for reasoning tasks (ARC-C, HellaSwag, WinoGrande).
FFN intermediate size (d_ffn) is the most important factor for knowledge- and math-oriented tasks (TruthfulQA, GSM8K).
Performance on ARC-C, HellaSwag, and WinoGrande is highly correlated, suggesting a shared reliance on reasoning ability.
MMLU is the most indicative benchmark for predicting a model's structural configuration.
Pruning layers with low Block Influence scores significantly degrades performance on reasoning tasks but has minimal effect on knowledge-focused tasks.
papers.limitation: The dataset may be biased towards certain model families (e.g., LLaMA) due to their overrepresentation in the open-source community.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across various domains, driving significant technological advancements and innovations. Despite the rapid growth in model scale and capability, systematic, data-driven research on how structural configurations affect performance remains scarce. To address this gap, we present a large-scale dataset encompassing diverse open-source LLM structures and their performance across multiple benchmarks. Leveraging this dataset, we conduct a systematic, data mining-driven analysis to validate and quantify the relationship between structural configurations and performance. Our study begins with a review of the historical development of LLMs and an exploration of potential future trends. We then analyze how various structural choices impact performance across benchmarks and further corroborate our findings using mechanistic interpretability techniques. By providing data-driven insights into LLM optimization, our work aims to guide the targeted development and application of future models. We will release our dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/DX0369/LLM-Structure-Performance-Dataset

papers.title: Interpretable LLM Guardrails via Sparse Representation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior to mitigate harmful, misleading, or biased content using sparse representation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SRS, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to disentangle activations into monosemantic features and steer LLM behavior via sparse steering vectors, achieving fine-grained control while preserving output quality.
papers.conclusion: SRS enables precise and interpretable steering of LLM behavior using sparse representations, providing a reliable guardrail for safety, fairness, and truthfulness with superior performance over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRS outperforms existing steering methods like CAA and SAE-TS in single-attribute and multi-attribute control tasks.
SRS maintains high linguistic quality, including grammatical correctness and language diversity, with minimal side effects.
SRS demonstrates robustness against diverse jailbreak prompts, achieving high defense rates.
Multi-attribute control with PCA composition strategy yields the best trade-off between control effectiveness and content quality.
Sparse features enable interpretable identification of attribute-relevant dimensions through KL divergence analysis.
papers.limitation: Multi-attribute steering strategies such as PCA may not fully capture complex relationships and conflicts between attributes.
future_direction: Layer-wise or component-wise multi-attribute steering to align interventions with semantic levels.
Context-aware and personalized steering based on semantic subdomains of prompts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities in generation tasks but are prone to producing harmful, misleading, or biased content, posing significant ethical and safety concerns. To mitigate such risks, representation engineering, which steer model behavior toward desired attributes by injecting carefully designed steering vectors into LLM's representations at inference time, has emerged as a promising alternative to fine-tuning approaches. However, due to the semantically entangled nature of LLM's representation, existing representation engineering methods still suffer from several limitations: limited fine-grained controllability, content quality degradation, and conflict in multi-attribute control. To overcome these challenges, we propose Sparse Representation Steering (SRS), a novel framework that achieves fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior by first disentangling internal activations into a sparse, semantically meaningful representation space, and then selectively steering relevant dimensions. Specifically, SRS leverages a pretrained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to transform dense, entangled activation patterns into a sparse monosemantic feature space. To identify relevant features, SRS contrasts sparse activations from positive and negative prompt pairs and measures their bidirectional KL divergence to locate dimensions most associated with the target attribute. We conduct comprehensive experiments on Gemma-2 series model across three alignment dimensions, i.e., safety, fairness, and truthfulness, to evaluate the effectiveness of SRS. Results show that SRS consistently outperforms existing steering methods, which achieves significantly improved controllability across both single and multiple attribute settings, while preserving high linguistic quality and general ability.

papers.title: CREME: Robustness Enhancement of Code LLMs via Layer-Aware Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of Code LLMs to natural language prompt perturbations via targeted, lightweight parameter updates (model editing)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CREME, a lightweight model editing framework that uses a single pair of original and perturbed prompts to identify robustness-sensitive layers via causal tracing and performs targeted parameter updates to align representations, enhancing model robustness to prompt perturbations.
papers.conclusion: CREME provides a practical, lightweight path to enhance the robustness of LLMs against real-world prompt variability without requiring full retraining or architectural modifications, and analysis of key layer distributions offers insights for future robustness-oriented interventions.
papers.key_findings:
CREME improves Pass@1 accuracy by 63% on perturbed prompts while maintaining stable performance on clean inputs (within ±1%).
Robustness-sensitive layers are primarily concentrated in the middle and deeper layers of the network, and their locations vary across different model architectures.
Causal tracing-based layer localization is critical for effective robustness enhancement.
CREME exhibits strong generalization across diverse perturbation types; editing based on a single instance restores up to 30% of overall accuracy within that perturbation category.
The method achieves an average G-RIR (generalization metric) of 30% across 20 perturbation types.
future_direction: Future work will explore extending CREME to broader task domains and evaluating its effectiveness against more challenging perturbations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in code generation, where the natural language prompt plays a crucial role in conveying user intent to the model. However, prior studies have shown that LLMs are highly sensitive to prompt perturbations. Minor modifications in wording, syntax, or formatting can significantly reduce the functional correctness of generated code. As perturbations frequently occur in real-world scenarios, improving the robustness of LLMs to prompt perturbations is essential for ensuring reliable performance in practical code generation. In this paper, we introduce CREME (Code Robustness Enhancement via Model Editing), a novel approach that enhances LLM robustness through targeted parameter updates. CREME first identifies robustness-sensitive layers by comparing hidden states between an original prompt and its perturbed variant. Then, it performs lightweight parameter editing at the identified layer to reduce performance degradation. We evaluate CREME on two widely used code generation benchmarks (HumanEval and MBPP) along with their perturbed counterparts. Experimental results show that CREME improves Pass@1 accuracy by 63% on perturbed prompts while maintaining stable performance on clean inputs, with accuracy deviations within 1%. Further analysis reveals that robustness-sensitive layers are primarily concentrated in the middle and deeper layers of the network, and their locations vary across different model architectures. These insights provide a valuable foundation for developing future robustness-oriented editing strategies.

papers.title: Beyond Surface Structure: A Causal Assessment of LLMs' Comprehension Ability
papers.research_question: Do LLMs genuinely comprehend deep structure for problem-solving, or do they primarily rely on learning surface structure?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes approximated direct and indirect causal effects (ADCE and AICE) to quantify LLMs' comprehension of deep vs. surface structure, finding that most LLMs exhibit deep structure comprehension, with closed-source models relying more on deep structure and open-source models being more surface-sensitive.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into LLMs' deep structure comprehension and offers novel methods (ADCE/AICE) for evaluating LLMs beyond surface-level accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Most tested LLMs exhibit deep structure comprehension ability, which grows with prediction accuracy.
Closed-source LLMs (e.g., GPT, Claude) rely more on deep structure, while open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama) are more surface-sensitive, with surface sensitivity decreasing with model scale.
ADCE provides a bidirectional evaluation of deep structure comprehension, assessing both sufficiency and necessity, offering a more comprehensive assessment than accuracy.
Fine-tuning (e.g., SFT, LoRA) enhances deep structure comprehension in models.
ADCE is more robust than accuracy in scenarios with spurious correlations, better reflecting reliance on deep structure.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capability in natural language tasks, yet debate persists on whether they truly comprehend deep structure (i.e., core semantics) or merely rely on surface structure (e.g., presentation format). Prior studies observe that LLMs' performance declines when intervening on surface structure, arguing their success relies on surface structure recognition. However, surface structure sensitivity does not prevent deep structure comprehension. Rigorously evaluating LLMs' capability requires analyzing both, yet deep structure is often overlooked. To this end, we assess LLMs' comprehension ability using causal mediation analysis, aiming to fully discover the capability of using both deep and surface structures. Specifically, we formulate the comprehension of deep structure as direct causal effect (DCE) and that of surface structure as indirect causal effect (ICE), respectively. To address the non-estimability of original DCE and ICE -- stemming from the infeasibility of isolating mutual influences of deep and surface structures, we develop the corresponding quantifiable surrogates, including approximated DCE (ADCE) and approximated ICE (AICE). We further apply the ADCE to evaluate a series of mainstream LLMs, showing that most of them exhibit deep structure comprehension ability, which grows along with the prediction accuracy. Comparing ADCE and AICE demonstrates closed-source LLMs rely more on deep structure, while open-source LLMs are more surface-sensitive, which decreases with model scale. Theoretically, ADCE is a bidirectional evaluation, which measures both the sufficiency and necessity of deep structure changes in causing output variations, thus offering a more comprehensive assessment than accuracy, a common evaluation in LLMs. Our work provides new insights into LLMs' deep structure comprehension and offers novel methods for LLMs evaluation.

papers.title: An X-Ray Is Worth 15 Features: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Radiology Report Generation
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be used to extract interpretable features from radiology images and generate accurate radiology reports without fine-tuning large vision-language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-Rad, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to decompose latent representations from a pre-trained vision transformer into interpretable features for radiology report generation, eliminating the need for fine-tuning large models.
papers.conclusion: SAEs can enhance multimodal reasoning in healthcare, providing a more interpretable alternative to existing VLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Rad achieves competitive radiology-specific metrics on the MIMIC-CXR dataset compared to state-of-the-art models while using significantly fewer computational resources.
SAE-Rad learns meaningful visual concepts and generates reports aligning closely with expert interpretations.
The hybrid SAE architecture achieves accurate latent reconstructions with comparable sparsity to state-of-the-art techniques.
SAE-Rad requires fewer edits and has lower significant clinical impact error rates in a radiologist reader study compared to baseline methods.
The framework demonstrates the utility of mechanistic interpretability for downstream tasks in healthcare.
papers.abstract: Radiological services are experiencing unprecedented demand, leading to increased interest in automating radiology report generation. Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from hallucinations, lack interpretability, and require expensive fine-tuning. We introduce SAE-Rad, which uses sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose latent representations from a pre-trained vision transformer into human-interpretable features. Our hybrid architecture combines state-of-the-art SAE advancements, achieving accurate latent reconstructions while maintaining sparsity. Using an off-the-shelf language model, we distil ground-truth reports into radiological descriptions for each SAE feature, which we then compile into a full report for each image, eliminating the need for fine-tuning large models for this task. To the best of our knowledge, SAE-Rad represents the first instance of using mechanistic interpretability techniques explicitly for a downstream multi-modal reasoning task. On the MIMIC-CXR dataset, SAE-Rad achieves competitive radiology-specific metrics compared to state-of-the-art models while using significantly fewer computational resources for training. Qualitative analysis reveals that SAE-Rad learns meaningful visual concepts and generates reports aligning closely with expert interpretations. Our results suggest that SAEs can enhance multimodal reasoning in healthcare, providing a more interpretable alternative to existing VLMs.

papers.title: Tackling Interpretability in Audio Classification Networks With Non-negative Matrix Factorization
papers.research_question: How to interpret decisions of audio classification networks in terms of high-level, listenable audio objects, and how to extend this to an inherently interpretable model with high performance?
papers.core_contribution: A framework for post-hoc and by-design interpretability in audio classification networks that uses Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to generate listenable, concept-based interpretations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively tackles interpretability for audio classification networks, providing listenable concept-based interpretations for both post-hoc and by-design settings.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed interpreter generates listenable audio interpretations by identifying relevant spectral components.
The method achieves high fidelity in approximating the classifier's output and demonstrates faithfulness through component removal experiments.
The by-design interpretable model (L2I_BD) achieves competitive performance compared to non-interpretable baselines and other interpretable models.
User studies confirm the usefulness and understandability of the generated audio interpretations.
Visualizations of interpretation relevances show clustering that aligns with human understanding of sound classes.
papers.limitation:
The system is more suited for traditional supervised classification tasks where identifying the importance of audio sources is useful; extending it to arbitrary audio processing tasks is a direction for future work.
Representing complex perceptually grounded audio concepts (e.g., 'shrill sounds') by a single component is challenging and may require a set of components.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other machine learning audio-based tasks.
Exploring dictionary learning or interpreter learning in few-shot data scenarios.
Investigating explicit representation of perceptually grounded audio concepts using sets of components.
papers.abstract: This paper tackles two major problem settings for interpretability of audio processing networks, post-hoc and by-design interpretation. For post-hoc interpretation, we aim to interpret decisions of a network in terms of high-level audio objects that are also listenable for the end-user. This is extended to present an inherently interpretable model with high performance. To this end, we propose a novel interpreter design that incorporates non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). In particular, an interpreter is trained to generate a regularized intermediate embedding from hidden layers of a target network, learnt as time-activations of a pre-learnt NMF dictionary. Our methodology allows us to generate intuitive audio-based interpretations that explicitly enhance parts of the input signal most relevant for a network's decision. We demonstrate our method's applicability on a variety of classification tasks, including multi-label data for real-world audio and music.

papers.title: Superposition disentanglement of neural representations reveals hidden alignment
papers.research_question: Does superposition interfere with representational alignment metrics, and does disentangling superposition via sparse autoencoders improve alignment scores?
papers.core_contribution: Superposition disentanglement via sparse autoencoders improves representational alignment metrics by revealing hidden feature correspondences that are obscured by different superposition arrangements.
papers.conclusion: Superposition disentanglement is necessary for mapping metrics to uncover true representational alignment, and this convergence opens new theoretical and empirical frontiers in understanding neural representations across artificial and biological networks.
papers.key_findings:
Toy models with different superposition arrangements show deflated alignment scores, which increase after SAE disentanglement.
Real DNNs (ResNet50 and ViT) show increased alignment after SAE disentanglement, especially in deeper layers.
Linear regression alignment improves when using SAE latents from the source to predict target neurons.
DNN-brain alignment improves when using SAE-disentangled DNN representations.
papers.limitation:
Cannot verify the superposition arrangement of the DNN features directly.
Inherits known SAE limitations, including feature consistency, absorption, and identifiability problems.
Limited DNN→DNN and DNN→brain alignment results presented.
future_direction: Scaling to diverse architectures, cross-architectural comparisons, additional brain datasets, and other domains like language processing.
Extending theory to encompass linear regression and neural geometry metrics like RSA.
Understanding the forces acting on superposition arrangements.
papers.abstract: The superposition hypothesis states that single neurons may participate in representing multiple features in order for the neural network to represent more features than it has neurons. In neuroscience and AI, representational alignment metrics measure the extent to which different deep neural networks (DNNs) or brains represent similar information. In this work, we explore a critical question: does superposition interact with alignment metrics in any undesirable way? We hypothesize that models which represent the same features in different superposition arrangements, i.e., their neurons have different linear combinations of the features, will interfere with predictive mapping metrics (semi-matching, soft-matching, linear regression), producing lower alignment than expected. We develop a theory for how permutation metrics are dependent on superposition arrangements. This is tested by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle superposition in toy models, where alignment scores are shown to typically increase when a model's base neurons are replaced with its sparse overcomplete latent codes. We find similar increases for DNN-DNN and DNN-brain linear regression alignment in the visual domain. Our results suggest that superposition disentanglement is necessary for mapping metrics to uncover the true representational alignment between neural networks.

papers.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the extent of feature space universality across large language models? Specifically, whether SAE feature spaces are similar under rotation-invariant transformations.
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that SAE feature spaces are similar across different LLMs, supporting the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which enables the transfer of interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that feature spaces are universal across LLMs, providing evidence for the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which can facilitate the transfer of interpretability techniques like steering vectors.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of LLMs show the highest similarity in SAE feature spaces, while layer 0 has low similarity.
Semantically meaningful subspaces, such as those for emotions or time, exhibit notable similarity across models.
The similarity is statistically significant as measured by SVCCA and RSA, with p-values below 0.05 for most layer pairs.
The approach works across various model pairs, including Pythia, Gemma, and Llama models.
Filtering non-concept features and many-to-1 mappings improves similarity scores.
papers.abstract: The Universality Hypothesis in large language models (LLMs) claims that different models converge towards similar concept representations in their latent spaces. Providing evidence for this hypothesis would enable researchers to exploit universal properties, facilitating the generalization of mechanistic interpretability techniques across models. Previous works studied if LLMs learned the same features, which are internal representations that activate on specific concepts. Since comparing features across LLMs is challenging due to polysemanticity, in which LLM neurons often correspond to multiple unrelated features rather than to distinct concepts, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been employed to disentangle LLM neurons into SAE features corresponding to distinct concepts. In this paper, we introduce a new variation of the universality hypothesis called Analogous Feature Universality: we hypothesize that even if SAEs across different models learn different feature representations, the spaces spanned by SAE features are similar, such that one SAE space is similar to another SAE space under rotation-invariant transformations. Evidence for this hypothesis would imply that interpretability techniques related to latent spaces, such as steering vectors, may be transferred across models via certain transformations. To investigate this hypothesis, we first pair SAE features across different models via activation correlation, and then measure spatial relation similarities between paired features via representational similarity measures, which transform spaces into representations that reveal hidden relational similarities. Our experiments demonstrate high similarities for SAE feature spaces across various LLMs, providing evidence for feature space universality.

papers.title: Feature-Guided SAE Steering for Refusal-Rate Control using Contrasting Prompts
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used with a systematic feature selection method to steer large language models for improved safety (refusal rate) without sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrasting prompts and a composite scoring function to systematically select Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features for steering, achieving simultaneous safety and utility improvements on Llama-3 8B without model retraining.
papers.conclusion: Feature-guided SAE steering is a viable and efficient approach to improving LLM safety without sacrificing utility, providing a foundation for mechanistically-informed safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
A composite scoring method using contrasting prompts can identify SAE features causally related to refusal behavior.
Steering the top-ranked feature (Feature 35831) improved safety performance by 18.9% and utility by 11.1%, overcoming the traditional safety-utility tradeoff.
The method provides a computationally efficient alternative to traditional safety alignment methods like RLHF and Constitutional AI, which require extensive retraining.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is restricted to Llama-3 8B and Layer 25, limiting understanding of scaling behaviors across architectures and transformer depths.
Reliance on automatic judges (GPT-4o for AirBench, GPT-4 for AlpacaEval 2.0) introduces potential limitations despite demonstrated correlation with human preferences.
The absence of direct comparisons with alternative steering methods limits the ability to establish relative effectiveness claims.
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) deployment requires guiding the LLM to recognize and not answer unsafe prompts while complying with safe prompts. Previous methods for achieving this require adjusting model weights along with other expensive procedures. While recent advances in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have enabled interpretable feature extraction from LLMs, existing approaches lack systematic feature selection methods and principled evaluation of safety-utility tradeoffs. We explored using different steering features and steering strengths using Sparse Auto Encoders (SAEs) to provide a solution. Using an accurate and innovative contrasting prompt method with the AI-Generated Prompts Dataset from teknium/OpenHermes-2p5-Mistral-7B and Air Bench eu-dataset to efficiently choose the best features in the model to steer, we tested this method on Llama-3 8B. We conclude that using this method, our approach achieves an 18.9% improvement in safety performance while simultaneously increasing utility by 11.1%, demonstrating that targeted SAE steering can overcome traditional safety-utility tradeoffs when optimal features are identified through principled selection methods.

papers.title: Explainable Molecular Property Prediction: Aligning Chemical Concepts with Predictions via Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property predictions using language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Lamole, a framework for explainable molecular property prediction that uses Group SELFIES representation and combines attention weights with gradients, calibrated by a marginal loss, to provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Lamole provides chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property prediction and can be integrated into an interpretable optimization pipeline for molecular design.
papers.key_findings:
Lamole achieves prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art baselines while improving explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%.
The proposed information flow-based explanation method, integrating attention and gradients, captures interactions between functional groups.
The marginal loss aligns explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, ensuring concept-aligned results.
Using only 10% of molecules with ground truth annotations can significantly improve explanation accuracy.
Integration with an evolutionary algorithm demonstrates Lamole's actionable utility for guiding molecular editing and optimization.
papers.limitation:
Complex interactions caused by multiple functional groups may not be fully captured, and other functional groups may receive relatively high importance scores.
The molecular editing case is a computational demonstration and does not imply real-world chemical optimality.
future_direction: Extending the framework to broader generalization scenarios, including unseen chemotypes.
Designing more strategies to reveal complex functional group interactions.
papers.abstract: Providing explainable molecular property predictions is critical for many scientific domains, such as drug discovery and material science. Though transformer-based language models have shown great potential in accurate molecular property prediction, they neither provide chemically meaningful explanations nor faithfully reveal the molecular structure-property relationships. In this work, we develop a framework for explainable molecular property prediction based on language models, dubbed as Lamole, which can provide chemical concepts-aligned explanations. We take a string-based molecular representation -- Group SELFIES -- as input tokens to pretrain and fine-tune our Lamole, as it provides chemically meaningful semantics. By disentangling the information flows of Lamole, we propose combining self-attention weights and gradients for better quantification of each chemically meaningful substructure's impact on the model's output. To make the explanations more faithfully respect the structure-property relationship, we then carefully craft a marginal loss to explicitly optimize the explanations to be able to align with the chemists' annotations. We bridge the manifold hypothesis with the elaborated marginal loss to prove that the loss can align the explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, leading to concept-aligned explanations. Experimental results over six mutagenicity datasets and one hepatotoxicity dataset demonstrate Lamole can achieve comparable classification accuracy and boost the explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%, being the state-of-the-art in explainable molecular property prediction.

papers.title: Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to formulate a statistical model for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations, and design an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and practical effectiveness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a statistical framework for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations and proposes Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and improved empirical performance.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a statistical framework and the GBA algorithm for provable feature recovery in SAEs, advancing mechanistic interpretability with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a statistical model that formalizes polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts.
Introduces Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm that uses bias adaptation to control neuron sparsity without hyperparameter tuning.
Provides the first provable recovery guarantee for an SAE algorithm, showing GBA recovers all monosemantic features under the statistical model.
Empirically demonstrates GBA achieves superior sparsity-loss trade-off and feature consistency on LLMs up to 1.5B parameters compared to baseline methods.
future_direction: Extending the statistical framework to more complex data distributions.
Scaling GBA to larger models.
Exploring applications in model steering and control.
papers.abstract: We study the challenge of achieving theoretically grounded feature recovery using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for the interpretation of Large Language Models. Existing SAE training algorithms often lack rigorous mathematical guarantees and suffer from practical limitations such as hyperparameter sensitivity and instability. To address these issues, we first propose a novel statistical framework for the feature recovery problem, which includes a new notion of feature identifiability by modeling polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts. Building on this framework, we introduce a new SAE training algorithm based on ``bias adaptation'', a technique that adaptively adjusts neural network bias parameters to ensure appropriate activation sparsity. We theoretically \highlight{prove that this algorithm correctly recovers all monosemantic features} when input data is sampled from our proposed statistical model. Furthermore, we develop an improved empirical variant, Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), and \highlight{demonstrate its superior performance against benchmark methods when applied to LLMs with up to 1.5 billion parameters}. This work represents a foundational step in demystifying SAE training by providing the first SAE algorithm with theoretical recovery guarantees, thereby advancing the development of more transparent and trustworthy AI systems through enhanced mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Beyond Label Attention: Transparency in Language Models for Automated Medical Coding via Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can dictionary learning be used to improve the interpretability of medical coding language models beyond label attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AutoCodeDL, a method that combines dictionary learning with label attention to provide more interpretable, dictionary-based rationales for ICD code predictions in medical language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that combining dictionary learning with label attention improves interpretability for medical coding models, providing a dictionary-based rationale for predictions and laying groundwork for future healthcare interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary learning can uncover hidden medical meanings in token embeddings, explaining why label attention highlights seemingly irrelevant tokens like stop words.
AutoCodeDL provides more precise explanations than label attention alone, as shown by a higher ratio of target code probability drop to non-target changes after ablation.
Learned dictionary features can steer model behavior, changing predictions for specific subsets of ICD codes without modifying model weights.
The dictionary features are human interpretable, demonstrating coherence and distinctiveness in automated and human evaluations.
Sparse autoencoders (L1 and SPINE) outperform baseline unsupervised methods in explainability and hidden meaning identification.
papers.limitation:
Sparse autoencoders cannot perfectly reconstruct PLM embeddings and thus cannot fully capture a model's downstream performance.
There exist dead or missing features in the dictionary, indicating not all features are useful or interpretable.
The sparse dictionaries learned are not as coherent as supervised mappings like LAAT, limiting human understandability.
Interpreting only the last layer PLM embeddings is insufficient for fully capturing and interpreting a PLM's behavior.
The resolution of dictionary features is lacking compared to the granularity of medical codes, suggesting features represent higher abstract concepts rather than highly-specific codes.
The applicability of scaling sparse autoencoders to smaller scale language datasets is unknown.
future_direction: Exploring more expressive representation learning techniques like causal and disentanglement methods for interpretability gains.
Unraveling complex relationships within medical PLMs through automated circuit discovery combined with dictionary learning.
Scaling up sparse autoencoders to potentially millions of dictionary features for extremely large language models.
papers.abstract: Medical coding, the translation of unstructured clinical text into standardized medical codes, is a crucial but time-consuming healthcare practice. Though large language models (LLM) could automate the coding process and improve the efficiency of such tasks, interpretability remains paramount for maintaining patient trust. Current efforts in interpretability of medical coding applications rely heavily on label attention mechanisms, which often leads to the highlighting of extraneous tokens irrelevant to the ICD code. To facilitate accurate interpretability in medical language models, this paper leverages dictionary learning that can efficiently extract sparsely activated representations from dense language model embeddings in superposition. Compared with common label attention mechanisms, our model goes beyond token-level representations by building an interpretable dictionary which enhances the mechanistic-based explanations for each ICD code prediction, even when the highlighted tokens are medically irrelevant. We show that dictionary features can steer model behavior, elucidate the hidden meanings of upwards of 90% of medically irrelevant tokens, and are human interpretable.

papers.title: Don't Forget It! Conditional Sparse Autoencoder Clamping Works for Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders be used to unlearn harmful knowledge in large language models while retaining safe knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a conditional SAE-based clamping method for unlearning that improves retention of safe information compared to prior SAE methods and performs comparably to RMU with better interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning outperforms prior SAE approaches on retention and performs comparably with RMU on forgetting harmful information while retaining safe information, with fewer hyperparameters and better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal Clamp achieves the lowest WMDP-bio accuracy (0.2718) and highest alignment score (0.8226), indicating effective unlearning with some impact on general knowledge.
Clamp Prime improves forgetting performance (WMDP-bio accuracy drops to 0.2985) but slightly reduces general knowledge retention compared to RMU.
Adversarial evaluation using Concurrent Greedy Search shows that unlearned models resist suffix attacks, continuing to output gibberish.
The method requires fewer hyperparameter choices than RMU while maintaining interpretability.
SAE-based unlearning is shown to be viable, with conditional steering reducing side effects on safe information.
papers.limitation:
Training sparse autoencoders and labeling the latents is slow and expensive, limiting practicality to models with pre-existing SAEs.
Steering models with sparse autoencoders requires closed weights, as attackers can remove steering hooks if they have access to the weights.
Using Wikitext as the retain set for RMU may cause bias, potentially inflating the method's score on biology-related subjects in evaluation.
future_direction: Investigating which SAE layers allow for the best unlearning.
Exploring the impact of latent space dimensionality (i.e., using SAEs with larger hidden activation shapes).
Training interpretable parameters that edit the SAE latent vector to allow for fully interpretable fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in Large Language Model (LLM) capabilities have brought great potential but also posed new risks. For example, LLMs with knowledge of bioweapons, advanced chemistry, or cyberattacks could cause violence if placed in the wrong hands or during malfunctions. Because of their nature as near-black boxes, intuitive interpretation of LLM internals remains an open research question, preventing developers from easily controlling model behavior and capabilities. The use of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) has recently emerged as a potential method of unraveling representations of concepts in LLMs internals, and has allowed developers to steer model outputs by directly modifying the hidden activations. In this paper, we use SAEs to identify unwanted concepts from the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset within gemma-2-2b internals and use feature steering to reduce the model's ability to answer harmful questions while retaining its performance on harmless queries. Our results bring back optimism to the viability of SAE-based explicit knowledge unlearning techniques.

papers.title: Understanding Chain-of-Thought in Large Language Models via Topological Data Analysis
papers.research_question: Why do different reasoning chains perform differently in reasoning, and what components of reasoning chains play a key role? This paper investigates these questions by analyzing reasoning chains from a structural perspective using topological data analysis.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces topological data analysis to evaluate reasoning chains structurally, finding that greater topological complexity during exploration correlates with higher accuracy, but successful final paths are topologically simpler with fewer redundant cycles.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a structural perspective on reasoning chain quality assessment using topological data analysis and offers guidance for future optimization of reasoning chains.
papers.key_findings:
Under the full-graph view, greater topological complexity (as measured by H0 and H1) correlates with higher accuracy.
Successful reasoning outcomes converge on simpler, more logical paths with reduced redundancy and minimal loops.
GoT (Graph of Thoughts) exhibits the richest topological structure and highest accuracy, while CoT is more linear with fewer loops and lower accuracy.
For the final path, accuracy is negatively correlated with topological complexity, indicating that successful paths are topologically simpler.
Topological data analysis provides a novel perspective for evaluating reasoning chain quality and reveals structural differences between reasoning paradigms.
papers.abstract: With the development of large language models (LLMs), particularly with the introduction of the long reasoning chain technique, the reasoning ability of LLMs in complex problem-solving has been significantly enhanced. While acknowledging the power of long reasoning chains, we cannot help but wonder: Why do different reasoning chains perform differently in reasoning? What components of the reasoning chains play a key role? Existing studies mainly focus on evaluating reasoning chains from a functional perspective, with little attention paid to their structural mechanisms. To address this gap, this work is the first to analyze and evaluate the quality of the reasoning chain from a structural perspective. We apply persistent homology from Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to map reasoning steps into semantic space, extract topological features, and analyze structural changes. These changes reveal semantic coherence, logical redundancy, and identify logical breaks and gaps. By calculating homology groups, we assess connectivity and redundancy at various scales, using barcode and persistence diagrams to quantify stability and consistency. Our results show that the topological structural complexity of reasoning chains correlates positively with accuracy. More complex chains identify correct answers sooner, while successful reasoning exhibits simpler topologies, reducing redundancy and cycles, enhancing efficiency and interpretability. This work provides a new perspective on reasoning chain quality assessment and offers guidance for future optimization.

papers.title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
papers.research_question: Do commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones?
papers.core_contribution: Common SAE metrics (e.g., auto-interpretability scores) do not reliably distinguish between trained and randomly initialized transformers, indicating these metrics are insufficient for validating interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: High aggregate auto-interpretability scores alone do not guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered; the paper recommends routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics similar to those from trained models.
Standard SAE quality metrics (explained variance, cosine similarity, L1 norm) show similar trends across trained and randomized variants.
Token distribution entropy reveals that features from randomized models remain simple and token-specific, unlike features from trained models which become more abstract across layers.
The area under the ROC curve (AUROC) for auto-interpretability tasks does not meaningfully discriminate between trained and randomized transformers in many settings.
Randomly initialized neural networks can preserve or amplify superposition present in input data, which may explain the similar SAE performance.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia models and the RedPajama dataset; results may vary with other architectures or data.
future_direction: Develop better metrics to distinguish between artifacts and genuinely learned computations in interpretability methods.
Investigate why randomly initialized transformers produce SAE metrics similar to trained ones, e.g., whether they preserve or amplify superposition.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to extract sparse, interpretable latents from transformer activations. We test whether commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines can distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones (e.g., where parameters are sampled i.i.d. from a Gaussian). Over a wide range of Pythia model sizes and multiple randomization schemes, we find that, in many settings, SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics that are similar to those from trained models. These results show that high aggregate auto-interpretability scores do not, by themselves, guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered. We therefore recommend treating common SAE metrics as useful but insufficient proxies for mechanistic interpretability and argue for routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.

papers.title: Superposition as Lossy Compression: Measure with Sparse Autoencoders and Connect to Adversarial Vulnerability
papers.research_question: How can superposition in neural networks be measured, and does superposition cause adversarial vulnerability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents an information-theoretic framework to measure superposition in neural networks using sparse autoencoders, and finds that adversarial training does not universally reduce superposition; its effect depends on task complexity and network capacity.
papers.conclusion: Superposition can be measured as lossy compression, and its relationship with adversarial vulnerability is nuanced, with adversarial training leading to feature expansion in low-complexity/high-capacity settings and feature reduction in high-complexity/low-capacity settings.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed superposition measure (ψ) strongly correlates with ground truth in toy models (r=0.94).
Dropout systematically reduces effective features and superposition.
Algorithmic tasks (e.g., multi-task sparse parity) show minimal superposition (ψ ≤ 1).
During grokking, a sharp drop in superposition occurs at the generalization transition.
Adversarial training can increase or decrease superposition depending on task complexity and network capacity, revealing abundance and scarcity regimes.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes SAE dictionary elements correspond one-to-one with genuine computational features, which can fail due to feature splitting, merging, or ghost features.
The linear representation assumption may be violated by hierarchical structure, gating mechanisms, or combinatorial feature interactions.
The magnitude-importance correspondence (|zi| reflects feature importance) may break if SAE reconstruction preserves irrelevant details or if feature importance is context-dependent.
The independent information assumption (Shannon entropy correctly aggregates information) fails when features are correlated, synergistic, or redundantly encoded.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other architectures and tasks.
Further investigate the connection between superposition and robustness.
Explore the implications for interpretability and adversarial defense.
papers.abstract: Neural networks achieve remarkable performance through superposition: encoding multiple features as overlapping directions in activation space rather than dedicating individual neurons to each feature. This challenges interpretability, yet we lack principled methods to measure superposition. We present an information-theoretic framework measuring a neural representation's effective degrees of freedom. We apply Shannon entropy to sparse autoencoder activations to compute the number of effective features as the minimum neurons needed for interference-free encoding. Equivalently, this measures how many "virtual neurons" the network simulates through superposition. When networks encode more effective features than actual neurons, they must accept interference as the price of compression. Our metric strongly correlates with ground truth in toy models, detects minimal superposition in algorithmic tasks, and reveals systematic reduction under dropout. Layer-wise patterns mirror intrinsic dimensionality studies on Pythia-70M. The metric also captures developmental dynamics, detecting sharp feature consolidation during grokking. Surprisingly, adversarial training can increase effective features while improving robustness, contradicting the hypothesis that superposition causes vulnerability. Instead, the effect depends on task complexity and network capacity: simple tasks with ample capacity allow feature expansion (abundance regime), while complex tasks or limited capacity force reduction (scarcity regime). By defining superposition as lossy compression, this work enables principled measurement of how neural networks organize information under computational constraints, connecting superposition to adversarial robustness.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can LLM confidence be accurately estimated by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by probing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS delivers an efficient, broadly applicable, and more accurate solution for estimating LLM confidence, thereby improving their trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% relative to the strongest prior method.
CCPS increases accuracy by 5 percentage points and AUROC by 6 percentage points on average.
CCPS demonstrates generalizability across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model sizes (8B to 32B).
CCPS outperforms baselines on both MMLU and MMLU-Pro benchmarks in multiple-choice and open-ended formats.
CCPS achieves significant improvements in Brier score and AUCPR.
papers.abstract: Miscalibration in Large Language Models (LLMs) undermines their reliability, highlighting the need for accurate confidence estimation. We introduce CCPS (Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability), a novel method analyzing internal representational stability in LLMs. CCPS applies targeted adversarial perturbations to final hidden states, extracts features reflecting the model's response to these perturbations, and uses a lightweight classifier to predict answer correctness. CCPS was evaluated on LLMs from 8B to 32B parameters (covering Llama, Qwen, and Mistral architectures) using MMLU and MMLU-Pro benchmarks in both multiple-choice and open-ended formats. Our results show that CCPS significantly outperforms current approaches. Across four LLMs and three MMLU variants, CCPS reduces Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% and Brier score by 21%, while increasing accuracy by 5 percentage points, Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve by 4 percentage points, and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve by 6 percentage points, all relative to the strongest prior method. CCPS delivers an efficient, broadly applicable, and more accurate solution for estimating LLM confidence, thereby improving their trustworthiness.

papers.title: eDIF: A European Deep Inference Fabric for Remote Interpretability of LLM
papers.research_question: Can an NDIF-compatible infrastructure be effectively deployed under European institutional, funding, and regulatory conditions, and how well does such a system support real-world interpretability workflows by academic users?
papers.core_contribution: This feasibility study demonstrates the viability and research value of a European NDIF-compatible interpretability cluster (eDIF), successfully supporting remote, structured interventions on large models and facilitating reproducible experimentation for a diverse group of researchers.
papers.conclusion: The study establishes a solid foundation for scaling eDIF into a pan-European resource, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and supporting the growing need for transparent, accessible AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
The eDIF system architecture proved stable and scalable, successfully provisioning models up to DeepSeek-R1-70B and supporting remote experimentation via the NNsight API.
User engagement increased steadily throughout the study, with high satisfaction ratings for onboarding and ease of use, and users reported significant time savings (10-50%) compared to local setups.
Technical challenges included prolonged download durations for activation data, intermittent execution interruptions, and inefficient GPU memory allocation due to an inability to share GPUs across models.
Migration experiments to an AMD-based HPC cluster demonstrated the general feasibility of operating NDIF on ROCm instead of CUDA, though structural challenges like Docker incompatibility and HPC scheduling constraints were encountered.
The study established a foundation for scaling eDIF into a pan-European resource, with strong user interest in sustained access and future developments like no-code interfaces and expanded model offerings.
papers.limitation:
Prolonged download durations for activation data and intermittent execution interruptions.
Absence of automatic GPU requirement estimation, requiring manual trial-and-error tuning for model deployments.
Inability to share GPUs across multiple models led to memory inefficiencies and a gap between theoretical GPU availability and effective resource utilization.
Docker-based setup was incompatible with HPC environments due to root access restrictions, requiring a partial migration to Apptainer which lacks full feature parity.
future_direction: Expanding the model repository to include modern, compact architectures such as Qwen and Gemma3, and enabling hot-swapping between models.
Developing no-code and low-code interfaces (e.g., visual tools, modular functional abstractions) to broaden accessibility and improve usability.
Establishing robust governance mechanisms including authentication, access control, fair-use scheduling policies, and GDPR-compliant data handling for multi-institutional use.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a feasibility study on the deployment of a European Deep Inference Fabric (eDIF), an NDIF-compatible infrastructure designed to support mechanistic interpretability research on large language models. The need for widespread accessibility of LLM interpretability infrastructure in Europe drives this initiative to democratize advanced model analysis capabilities for the research community. The project introduces a GPU-based cluster hosted at Ansbach University of Applied Sciences and interconnected with partner institutions, enabling remote model inspection via the NNsight API. A structured pilot study involving 16 researchers from across Europe evaluated the platform's technical performance, usability, and scientific utility. Users conducted interventions such as activation patching, causal tracing, and representation analysis on models including GPT-2 and DeepSeek-R1-70B. The study revealed a gradual increase in user engagement, stable platform performance throughout, and a positive reception of the remote experimentation capabilities. It also marked the starting point for building a user community around the platform. Identified limitations such as prolonged download durations for activation data as well as intermittent execution interruptions are addressed in the roadmap for future development. This initiative marks a significant step towards widespread accessibility of LLM interpretability infrastructure in Europe and lays the groundwork for broader deployment, expanded tooling, and sustained community collaboration in mechanistic interpretability research.

papers.title: Measuring Progress in Dictionary Learning for Language Model Interpretability with Board Game Models
papers.research_question: How can we measure progress in interpretable dictionary learning for language models? The paper proposes using board game models with known interpretable features as a testbed to evaluate sparse autoencoder quality.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces board game models as a testbed for evaluating sparse autoencoders, proposes two new metrics (coverage and board reconstruction) for SAE quality, and introduces p-annealing, a training technique that improves SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a more objective paradigm for evaluating SAE quality with coverage and board reconstruction metrics, and shows that p-annealing improves SAE training.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can accurately reconstruct game boards, though they do not match linear probe performance.
Standard SAEs trained with p-annealing perform on par with Gated SAEs on existing metrics and show improvement on the new metrics.
Coverage and board reconstruction metrics reveal differences in SAE quality not captured by unsupervised metrics like L0 and loss recovered.
The metrics are optimal in the elbow region of the Pareto frontier, validating common wisdom about SAE quality.
papers.limitation:
The metrics are confined to chess and Othello domains, raising concerns about generalizability.
The set of board state properties is determined by researchers based on domain knowledge, potentially overlooking essential features.
The evaluation does not directly address how learned features could be used for downstream interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: What latent features are encoded in language model (LM) representations? Recent work on training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle interpretable features in LM representations has shown significant promise. However, evaluating the quality of these SAEs is difficult because we lack a ground-truth collection of interpretable features that we expect good SAEs to recover. We thus propose to measure progress in interpretable dictionary learning by working in the setting of LMs trained on chess and Othello transcripts. These settings carry natural collections of interpretable features -- for example, "there is a knight on F3" -- which we leverage into $\textit{supervised}$ metrics for SAE quality. To guide progress in interpretable dictionary learning, we introduce a new SAE training technique, $\textit{p-annealing}$, which improves performance on prior unsupervised metrics as well as our new metrics.

papers.title: Evolution of SAE Features Across Layers in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do SAE features evolve across layers in transformer-based language models? Specifically, what are the statistical relationships between features in adjacent layers, and how are features passed through, combined, or specialized?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a vertical feature graph to connect SAE features across adjacent layers based on correlation measures, and provides a web interface to explore the graph. It finds that features can be passed through layers, combined like logic gates, or become more specialized.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that SAE features in different layers have clear relationships, and the graph visualization helps understand these. Communities of features include logic gates and passed-through features, and the graph can enrich or verify future autointerp methods.
papers.key_findings:
A considerable amount of features are passed through from a previous layer.
Some features can be expressed as quasi-boolean combinations (AND/OR gates) of previous features.
Some features become more specialized in later layers.
The feature graph can be used to spot incorrect GPT-3.5-generated autointerp explanations.
Correlational relationships often but not always correspond to causal relationships, as shown by ablation checks.
papers.limitation:
The approach measures correlation, not causation.
Sparse activations lead to few co-activations, which might cause spurious correlations.
Only four similarity measures are used; other measures might yield different results.
Hyperparameters (activation and similarity thresholds) are crucial and affect interpretability.
Community detection algorithms are general-purpose; specialized algorithms might find more semantically valid communities.
Reliance on GPT-3.5 summaries which can be inaccurate.
Lack of a theory describing how feature specialization occurs.
future_direction: Using a combination of statistical and geometric measures to improve results.
Applying specialized community-detection algorithms for sparse multipartite graphs.
Developing a theory for how feature specialization occurs and comparing SAE decoder weights for general vs. specific features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders for transformer-based language models are typically defined independently per layer. In this work we analyze statistical relationships between features in adjacent layers to understand how features evolve through a forward pass. We provide a graph visualization interface for features and their most similar next-layer neighbors (https://stefanhex.com/spar-2024/feature-browser/), and build communities of related features across layers. We find that a considerable amount of features are passed through from a previous layer, some features can be expressed as quasi-boolean combinations of previous features, and some features become more specialized in later layers.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: On the Emergence and Test-Time Use of Structural Information in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models learn abstract structures and utilize the learnt structural information at test-time?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the emergence of structural information during learning correlates with complex reasoning tasks, and that the ability to perform test-time compositional generation remains limited.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can learn structural information during fine-tuning, but their ability to flexibly re-compose out-of-distribution to produce new knowledge is limited. MLP sublayers are more important for syntactic transformations and the separation between concepts emerges during training and is linearly encoded.
papers.key_findings:
The emergence of learning structural information correlates with complex reasoning tasks.
The ability to perform test-time compositional generation remains limited.
Models capture distinct internal representations for different syntactic transformations, and these representations become more separable during training.
MLP blocks contribute more to syntactic transformation success than attention mechanisms.
The probability of predicting the correct token for a transformation increases sharply in the final third of the network.
papers.limitation:
Focus only on English transformations, limiting generalizability to cross-linguistic patterns.
Single-level transformation approach may conflate multiple sub-operations.
Findings on an 8B model may not generalize to larger scales.
future_direction: Cross-linguistic studies.
Finer-grained operation decomposition.
Evaluation on larger models with appropriately challenging transformation tasks.
papers.abstract: Learning structural information from observational data is central to producing new knowledge outside the training corpus. This holds for mechanistic understanding in scientific discovery as well as flexible test-time compositional generation. We thus study how language models learn abstract structures and utilize the learnt structural information at test-time. To ensure a controlled setup, we design a natural language dataset based on linguistic structural transformations. We empirically show that the emergence of learning structural information correlates with complex reasoning tasks, and that the ability to perform test-time compositional generation remains limited.

papers.title: Evaluating Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graph Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we effectively evaluate graph self-supervised learning (GSSL) methods for molecular graph embeddings, given that their broad applicability complicates evaluation and current downstream datasets may not provide a complete picture?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MOLGRAPH EVAL, a benchmark for evaluating molecular graph embeddings from GSSL methods via a suite of probing tasks, revealing significant inconsistencies between inferences from existing downstream datasets and more nuanced probing.
papers.conclusion: MOLGRAPH EVAL provides a more comprehensive and nuanced evaluation of GSSL methods for molecular graphs, uncovering limitations of current evaluation methodologies that rely solely on downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
All GSSL methods improve molecular property prediction (MPP) over random initialization, but the performance gain varies with dataset size.
Rankings of GSSL methods differ between using fixed embeddings (probing) and fine-tuned embeddings, indicating probing alone is not a definitive indicator for fine-tuning performance.
Optimal pre-training hyperparameters for fixed and fine-tuned embeddings often differ, suggesting that probing fixed embeddings may not reflect true downstream performance after fine-tuning.
Randomly initialized embeddings outperform almost every GSSL method on node- and pair-level topological metrics, indicating GSSL methods are not universally better and random features can be useful for local geometry tasks.
Substructure detection performance correlates well with MPP performance, suggesting that GSSL methods' superiority in MPP may be attributed to their capacity for substructure awareness.
papers.limitation:
The benchmark is limited to the nine studied GSSL methods and the molecular datasets used; extending to more methods and datasets is needed for broader conclusions.
Potential ethical concerns include bias and fairness in the datasets, dual use for designing harmful substances, environmental impact of training, and privacy issues.
future_direction: Extend the benchmark to incorporate more GSSL methods and larger datasets (e.g., ZINC15).
Investigate why optimal pre-training configurations for probing and fine-tuning differ.
Explore the reasons behind the strong performance of randomly initialized embeddings on local topological metrics.
papers.abstract: Graph Self-Supervised Learning (GSSL) provides a robust pathway for acquiring embeddings without expert labelling, a capability that carries profound implications for molecular graphs due to the staggering number of potential molecules and the high cost of obtaining labels. However, GSSL methods are designed not for optimisation within a specific domain but rather for transferability across a variety of downstream tasks. This broad applicability complicates their evaluation. Addressing this challenge, we present "Molecular Graph Representation Evaluation" (MOLGRAPHEVAL), generating detailed profiles of molecular graph embeddings with interpretable and diversified attributes. MOLGRAPHEVAL offers a suite of probing tasks grouped into three categories: (i) generic graph, (ii) molecular substructure, and (iii) embedding space properties. By leveraging MOLGRAPHEVAL to benchmark existing GSSL methods against both current downstream datasets and our suite of tasks, we uncover significant inconsistencies between inferences drawn solely from existing datasets and those derived from more nuanced probing.
