We open source a library at https://github.com/UFO-101/auto-circuit that includes highly efficient implementations of a wide range of ablation methodologies and circuit discovery algorithms.

papers.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable monosemantic features from polysemantic activations in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes PS-Eval, a new evaluation metric and dataset for assessing whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations. It finds that SAEs optimized for MSE-L0 Pareto frontier do not necessarily improve monosemantic feature extraction, and that deeper layers and attention mechanisms contribute to distinguishing polysemous words.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes Poly-Semantic Evaluation (PS-Eval), a new metric and dataset to assess the ability of SAEs to extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations, in complement to traditional MSE or L0 metrics. The work encourages the community to conduct holistic evaluations of SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability and do not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features.
Deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word.
Increasing the latent dimension of SAEs generally improves specificity up to a saturation point.
Activation functions like TopK and JumpReLU, designed to improve MSE-L0 trade-off, do not perform well on PS-Eval metrics; ReLU performs best.
SAE features are more interpretable than raw LLM activations for polysemous words.
papers.limitation: PS-Eval relies on evaluating the maximum activation of SAE features, which may not always align with intended word meanings and could introduce ambiguity.
future_direction: Incorporate similarity metrics that utilize the distribution of SAE features, rather than relying solely on maximum activation.
Extend PS-Eval beyond natural language to other domains such as diffusion models and vision-language models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have gained a lot of attention as a promising tool to improve the interpretability of large language models (LLMs) by mapping the complex superposition of polysemantic neurons into monosemantic features and composing a sparse dictionary of words. However, traditional performance metrics like Mean Squared Error and L0 sparsity ignore the evaluation of the semantic representational power of SAEs -- whether they can acquire interpretable monosemantic features while preserving the semantic relationship of words. For instance, it is not obvious whether a learned sparse feature could distinguish different meanings in one word. In this paper, we propose a suite of evaluations for SAEs to analyze the quality of monosemantic features by focusing on polysemous words. Our findings reveal that SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability, which does not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features. The analysis of SAEs with polysemous words can also figure out the internal mechanism of LLMs; deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word. Our semantics focused evaluation offers new insights into the polysemy and the existing SAE objective and contributes to the development of more practical SAEs.

papers.title: SynthSAEBench: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Scalable Realistic Synthetic Data
papers.research_question: How can we create a scalable synthetic benchmark with ground-truth features to evaluate and diagnose Sparse Autoencoder architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SynthSAEBench, a toolkit and benchmark for generating large-scale synthetic data with realistic feature characteristics (correlation, hierarchy, superposition) to evaluate and diagnose Sparse Autoencoder architectures.
papers.conclusion: SynthSAEBench complements LLM benchmarks by providing ground-truth features and controlled ablations, enabling precise diagnosis of SAE failure modes and validation of architectural improvements before scaling to LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Reproduces LLM SAE phenomena: Matryoshka SAEs overperform on probing despite poor reconstruction; MP-SAEs overperform on reconstruction but poor probing; poor SAE probing relative to supervised probes; precision-recall trade-off mediated by L0.
Identifies a new failure mode: MP-SAEs exploit superposition noise to improve reconstruction without learning ground-truth features, suggesting expressive encoders can overfit.
No SAE architecture achieves perfect performance on SynthSAEBench-16k, highlighting a target for architectural improvement.
papers.limitation: The synthetic model cannot capture all aspects of real neural network representations.
future_direction: Extend the framework to Minkowski representations and feature manifolds.
Understand the performance gap between JumpReLU and BatchTopK SAEs.
papers.abstract: Improving Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) requires benchmarks that can precisely validate architectural innovations. However, current SAE benchmarks on LLMs are often too noisy to differentiate architectural improvements, and current synthetic data experiments are too small-scale and unrealistic to provide meaningful comparisons. We introduce SynthSAEBench, a toolkit for generating large-scale synthetic data with realistic feature characteristics including correlation, hierarchy, and superposition, and a standardized benchmark model, SynthSAEBench-16k, enabling direct comparison of SAE architectures. Our benchmark reproduces several previously observed LLM SAE phenomena, including the disconnect between reconstruction and latent quality metrics, poor SAE probing results, and a precision-recall trade-off mediated by L0. We further use our benchmark to identify a new failure mode: Matching Pursuit SAEs exploit superposition noise to improve reconstruction without learning ground-truth features, suggesting that more expressive encoders can easily overfit. SynthSAEBench complements LLM benchmarks by providing ground-truth features and controlled ablations, enabling researchers to precisely diagnose SAE failure modes and validate architectural improvements before scaling to LLMs.

papers.title: Efficient Dictionary Learning with Switch Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders efficiently to reduce compute cost while maintaining performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture that uses a mixture-of-experts style routing to reduce compute cost and memory bottlenecks while maintaining reconstruction performance and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Switch SAEs are a promising approach for scaling sparse autoencoders, providing a Pareto improvement in FLOPs vs. MSE without significant reduction in feature interpretability, and may enable large-scale SAE training on GPU clusters.
papers.key_findings:
Switch SAEs achieve better reconstruction than dense TopK SAEs at a fixed compute budget (FLOP-matched).
Switch SAEs require more total features (parameters) to achieve the same reconstruction as dense SAEs when trained to convergence, but this gap narrows for larger SAEs.
In FLOP-matched settings, Switch SAEs Pareto-dominate TopK, Gated, and ReLU SAEs in terms of reconstruction MSE and fraction of loss recovered.
Switch SAEs exhibit feature duplication across experts, which reduces capacity, but this effect diminishes at larger sparsities.
Switch SAE features are as interpretable as TopK SAE features in FLOP-matched settings, and in width-matched settings they have higher true positive rates but lower true negative rates in automated interpretability detection.
papers.limitation:
Switch SAEs have reduced performance at a fixed number of parameters compared to dense SAEs, especially for attention and MLP layers.
Only the simplest mixture-of-experts architecture is investigated, leaving open the question of maximum performance gain from more sophisticated MoE architectures.
No downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs (e.g., feature steering or circuit discovery) are conducted.
future_direction: Investigate feature deduplication techniques, more sophisticated routing architectures, and multiple active experts.
Explore more sophisticated mixture-of-experts architectures like GShard, DeepSeekMoE, and expert choice routing.
Conduct downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs, such as feature steering or circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a recent technique for decomposing neural network activations into human-interpretable features. However, in order for SAEs to identify all features represented in frontier models, it will be necessary to scale them up to very high width, posing a computational challenge. In this work, we introduce Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture aimed at reducing the compute cost of training SAEs. Inspired by sparse mixture of experts models, Switch SAEs route activation vectors between smaller "expert" SAEs, enabling SAEs to efficiently scale to many more features. We present experiments comparing Switch SAEs with other SAE architectures, and find that Switch SAEs deliver a substantial Pareto improvement in the reconstruction vs. sparsity frontier for a given fixed training compute budget. We also study the geometry of features across experts, analyze features duplicated across experts, and verify that Switch SAE features are as interpretable as features found by other SAE architectures.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Understanding of Identifiable Sparse Autoencoders and Beyond
papers.research_question: Can SAEs recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the polysemantic inputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical framework showing that standard Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) generally fail to fully recover ground-truth monosemantic features unless they are extremely sparse, and proposes a reweighted SAE (WSAE) that improves feature recovery by adaptively weighting dimensions based on their polysemantic level.
papers.conclusion: SAEs have inherent limits and cannot fully disentangle features under realistic sparsity; they should be regarded as an approximation tool. The proposed WSAE enhances feature recovery and interpretability in low-sparsity scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs generally fail to fully recover ground truth monosemantic features due to feature shrinking and feature vanishing.
SAEs can fully recover ground truth features only under the condition of extreme sparsity.
The proposed Weighted Sparse Autoencoder (WSAE) narrows the gap between polysemantic feature reconstruction and ground truth feature reconstruction, leading to better recovery.
Experiments on synthetic data validate the theoretical findings on sparsity and the improvement from reweighting.
Experiments on real language (Pythia, Llama) and vision (ResNet) models show that WSAE enhances feature monosemanticity and interpretability compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation: SAE-based interpretability should be regarded as an approximation tool, not as a faithful feature recovery mechanism, because full disentanglement is mathematically impossible under realistic sparsity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting features learned by large language models (LLMs). It aims to recover complex superposed polysemantic features into interpretable monosemantic ones through feature reconstruction via sparsely activated neural networks. Despite the wide applications of SAEs, it remains unclear under what conditions an SAE can fully recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the superposed polysemantic ones. In this paper, through theoretical analysis, we for the first time propose the necessary and sufficient conditions for identifiable SAEs (SAEs that learn unique and ground truth monosemantic features), including 1) extreme sparsity of the ground truth feature, 2) sparse activation of SAEs, and 3) enough hidden dimensions of SAEs. Moreover, when the identifiable conditions are not fully met, we propose a reweighting strategy to improve the identifiability. Specifically, following the theoretically suggested weight selection principle, we prove that the gap between the loss functions of SAE reconstruction and monosemantic feature reconstruction can be narrowed, so that the reweighted SAEs have better reconstruction of the ground truth monosemantic features than the uniformly weighted ones. In experiments, we validate our theoretical findings and show that our weighted SAE significantly improves feature monosemanticity and interpretability.

papers.title: Optimizing Soft Prompt Tuning via Structural Evolution
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and performance of soft prompt tuning by analyzing and optimizing the structural evolution of soft prompt representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a topological analysis framework for soft prompt tuning and introduces TSLoss, a loss function that regularizes the topological structure of prompt embeddings to improve convergence and performance.
papers.conclusion: TSLoss provides an interpretable framework for understanding and optimizing soft prompt tuning from a topological perspective, enhancing convergence and performance.
papers.key_findings:
Topologically stable and compact soft prompts achieve better downstream performance.
TSLoss accelerates convergence and improves tuning performance across models and datasets.
The training process of soft prompt tuning maintains basic connectivity while loops and redundant structures gradually disappear.
TSLoss enhances both convergence efficiency and final accuracy.
The structural evolution of soft prompts can be quantified using persistent homology from topological data analysis.
future_direction: Future work will explore the relationship between structural evolution in the prompt parameter space and its semantic effects, aiming to further enhance interpretability and generalization.
papers.abstract: Soft prompt tuning leverages continuous embeddings to capture task-specific information in large pre-trained language models (LLMs), achieving competitive performance in few-shot settings. However, soft prompts rely on high-dimensional, implicit representations and lack explicit semantics and traceable training behaviors, which limits their interpretability. To address this limitation, we propose a soft prompt tuning optimization method based on topological morphological evolution. Specifically, we employ persistent homology from topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify the structural representations of soft prompts in continuous parameter space and their training process evolution. Quantitative analysis shows that topologically stable and compact soft prompts achieve better downstream performance. Based on this empirical observation, we construct a loss function for optimizing soft prompt tuning, termed Topological Soft Prompt Loss (TSLoss). TSLoss guides the model to learn structurally stable adaptations by quantifying inter-parameter connectivity and redundancy. Extensive experiments show that training with TSLoss accelerates convergence and improves tuning performance, providing an interpretable method to understand and optimize soft prompt tuning from structural and topological perspectives.

papers.title: Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the reconstruction fidelity of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at a given sparsity level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces JumpReLU SAEs, a simple modification of ReLU SAEs that achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level and is similarly interpretable to other SAE methods.
papers.conclusion: JumpReLU SAEs are a mild improvement over prevailing SAE training methodologies, offering better or equal reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity, similar interpretability, and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
JumpReLU SAEs consistently provide more faithful reconstructions than Gated SAEs and at least as good as, and often slightly better than, TopK SAEs at a given sparsity level.
JumpReLU SAEs have few dead features without the need for resampling during training.
JumpReLU SAEs have a similar proportion of very high frequency features (active on >10% of tokens) as TopK SAEs, which is higher than Gated SAEs.
Manual and automated interpretability studies show that JumpReLU SAE features are similarly interpretable to Gated and TopK SAE features.
JumpReLU SAEs are efficient to train, requiring no auxiliary loss terms and having an elementwise activation function (unlike TopK).
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are conducted on a single model (Gemma 2 9B), raising uncertainty about transfer to other models.
The science of principled evaluations of SAE performance is still in its infancy; it is unclear how well current metrics correlate with downstream utility.
JumpReLU SAEs tend to have relatively more very high frequency features than Gated SAEs.
JumpReLU SAEs introduce new hyperparameters (initial threshold and bandwidth) that require selection.
future_direction: Evaluate SAEs on a broader selection of metrics that more directly correspond to the value SAEs add by aiding or enabling downstream tasks, such as circuit analysis or model control.
Further tweak the loss function used to train JumpReLU SAEs to directly tackle the phenomenon of high frequency features.
Develop more principled ways to choose hyperparameters, such as the bandwidth parameter, possibly borrowing from kernel density estimation literature.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising unsupervised approach for identifying causally relevant and interpretable linear features in a language model's (LM) activations. To be useful for downstream tasks, SAEs need to decompose LM activations faithfully; yet to be interpretable the decomposition must be sparse -- two objectives that are in tension. In this paper, we introduce JumpReLU SAEs, which achieve state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level on Gemma 2 9B activations, compared to other recent advances such as Gated and TopK SAEs. We also show that this improvement does not come at the cost of interpretability through manual and automated interpretability studies. JumpReLU SAEs are a simple modification of vanilla (ReLU) SAEs -- where we replace the ReLU with a discontinuous JumpReLU activation function -- and are similarly efficient to train and run. By utilising straight-through-estimators (STEs) in a principled manner, we show how it is possible to train JumpReLU SAEs effectively despite the discontinuous JumpReLU function introduced in the SAE's forward pass. Similarly, we use STEs to directly train L0 to be sparse, instead of training on proxies such as L1, avoiding problems like shrinkage.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: Attacking Superposition with Dictionary Learning Features as The Simplest Factorization Dictionary Learning Worries Fractional Dimensionality and Pressure The Two Circle Phenomenon in Memorization Weight Superposition Attention Head Superposition Feature Manifold Toy Model
papers.research_question: How can dictionary learning be used to extract features from superposition in neural networks, and what are the challenges and insights from toy models?
papers.core_contribution: The blog presents developing ideas on using dictionary learning to attack superposition in neural networks, with conceptual contributions on feature factorization, geometry, and challenges in extracting interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: These are preliminary research notes sharing ongoing work on superposition and dictionary learning, with the aim of building infrastructure for larger-scale investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary learning solutions 'bounce' when the dictionary size matches the true number of features in synthetic data, as shown by plotting Mean Squared Error vs Total Information.
Dictionary learning may be too strong for neural networks due to concerns like compressed sensing allowing arbitrary functions and non-zero-centered representations.
Feature pressure and training duration affect the geometry of superposition in toy models, leading to uniform polyhedra or other structures.
Attention heads can implement skip-trigram circuits in superposition, meaning circuits can be distributed across multiple heads, cautioning against studying heads in isolation.
Feature manifolds in toy models show emergent discretization, where continuous manifolds are represented by discrete neurons, similar to value coding in neuroscience.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be too strong for neural networks because compressed sensing algorithms allow arbitrary functions, which might not align with how networks cheaply retrieve features.
The representation may not be zero-centered, which typical dictionary learning algorithms do not handle well.
The smallest length scale discretization in feature manifold toy models may be an optimization failure.
future_direction: Systematic, large-scale investigation of superposition in real models using dictionary learning.
Additional research to understand the emergent discretization in feature manifolds.
papers.abstract: How can dictionary learning be used to extract features from superposition in neural networks, and what are the challenges and insights from toy models? The blog presents developing ideas on using dictionary learning to attack superposition in neural networks, with conceptual contributions on feature factorization, geometry, and challenges in extracting interpretable features. These are preliminary research notes sharing ongoing work on superposition and dictionary learning, with the aim of building infrastructure for larger-scale investigations.

papers.title: BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can relaxing the top-k constraint in sparse autoencoders to a batch-level constraint, allowing a variable number of latents per sample, improve reconstruction without sacrificing average sparsity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BatchTopK SAEs, a training method that improves upon TopK SAEs by relaxing the per-sample top-k constraint to a batch-level constraint, allowing variable latents per sample and improving reconstruction without sacrificing average sparsity.
papers.conclusion: BatchTopK SAEs are an effective variant of TopK SAEs that improve reconstruction by allowing a variable number of latents per sample, and small modifications to the activation function can significantly impact SAE performance.
papers.key_findings:
BatchTopK SAEs consistently outperform TopK SAEs in reconstructing activations from GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B.
BatchTopK SAEs achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art JumpReLU SAEs on GPT-2 Small and outperform them in some settings on Gemma 2 2B.
BatchTopK allows direct specification of the average number of active latents, unlike JumpReLU SAEs which require costly hyperparameter tuning to target a specific sparsity.
BatchTopK activates a variable number of latents per sample, using few latents for simple samples (e.g., <BOS>-token) and many for complex ones.
The method uses a global threshold during inference to remove batch dependency, enabling practical use.
papers.limitation:
The paper did not directly assess the human interpretability of the latents learned by BatchTopK SAEs, though architectural similarity to TopK SAEs suggests they would remain comparably interpretable.
On Gemma 2 2B, BatchTopK only outperforms JumpReLU SAEs in terms of cross-entropy degradation in the lowest sparsity setting (k=16).
future_direction: Future work is expected to continue finding improvements that better approximate the latent structure of model activations.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting language model activations by decomposing them into sparse, interpretable features. A popular approach is the TopK SAE, that uses a fixed number of the most active latents per sample to reconstruct the model activations. We introduce BatchTopK SAEs, a training method that improves upon TopK SAEs by relaxing the top-k constraint to the batch-level, allowing for a variable number of latents to be active per sample. As a result, BatchTopK adaptively allocates more or fewer latents depending on the sample, improving reconstruction without sacrificing average sparsity. We show that BatchTopK SAEs consistently outperform TopK SAEs in reconstructing activations from GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B, and achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art JumpReLU SAEs. However, an advantage of BatchTopK is that the average number of latents can be directly specified, rather than approximately tuned through a costly hyperparameter sweep. We provide code for training and evaluating BatchTopK SAEs at https://github.com/bartbussmann/BatchTopK

papers.title: Simple LLM Baselines are Competitive for Model Diffing
papers.research_question: How do existing API-only model diffing methods (LLM-based and SAE-based) compare in terms of generalization, interestingness, and abstraction level of the hypotheses they generate?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an evaluation framework with metrics for generalization, interestingness, and abstraction level for model diffing methods, and finds that an improved LLM-based baseline performs comparably to an SAE-based method while typically surfacing more abstract behavioral differences.
papers.conclusion: Simple LLM-based approaches remain a strong baseline for model diffing research, performing comparably to SAE-based methods while producing more abstract hypotheses.
papers.key_findings:
An improved LLM-based model diffing baseline performs comparably to an SAE-based method on generalization (accuracy, frequency) and interestingness metrics.
The LLM-based method consistently produces hypotheses at a higher abstraction level than the SAE-based method.
Both methods can surface previously undocumented behavioral differences, such as formatting and stylistic shifts between model revisions.
API-only model diffing methods cannot surface behavioral differences that do not manifest in model outputs on the given prompt distribution.
The proposed evaluation metrics (frequency, accuracy, interestingness, abstraction level) help disentangle distinct aspects of hypothesis quality.
papers.limitation:
Automatic evaluation has inherent limitations: LLM judges can be unreliable, and the proposed metrics cannot guarantee hypothesis quality.
The framework only evaluates discovered hypotheses; it cannot assess if true differences go undetected.
Discovered differences depend on the prompt distribution; using WildChat may miss domain-specific differences.
API-only methods can only surface differences exhibited in model outputs; differences that do not manifest cannot be detected.
future_direction: Hybrid approaches that combine SAE-based feature detection with LLM-based summarization.
Targeted prompt curation to increase sensitivity to specific behaviors of interest.
Applying diffing methods to compare reasoning behavior (e.g., chain-of-thought strategies) across models.
papers.abstract: Standard LLM evaluations only test capabilities or dispositions that evaluators designed them for, missing unexpected differences such as behavioral shifts between model revisions or emergent misaligned tendencies. Model diffing addresses this limitation by automatically surfacing systematic behavioral differences. Recent approaches include LLM-based methods that generate natural language descriptions and sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based methods that identify interpretable features. However, no systematic comparison of these approaches exists nor are there established evaluation criteria. We address this gap by proposing evaluation metrics for key desiderata (generalization, interestingness, and abstraction level) and use these to compare existing methods. Our results show that an improved LLM-based baseline performs comparably to the SAE-based method while typically surfacing more abstract behavioral differences.

papers.title: Attribution assignment for deep-generative sequence models enables interpretability analysis using positive-only data
papers.research_question: How can we interpret generative sequence models trained on positive-only data to extract biological insights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces GAMA, an attribution method based on Integrated Gradients, to enable interpretability of autoregressive generative models trained on positive-only data, allowing for the extraction of biologically relevant motifs without negative examples.
papers.conclusion: GAMA provides a novel method for interpreting generative sequence models, enabling the discovery of binding motifs and enhancing trust in model-generated sequences for applications like antibody design.
papers.key_findings:
GAMA can recover implanted motifs in synthetic datasets with high accuracy, especially at high signal-to-noise ratios.
GAMA's performance is robust to the position of motifs in sequences.
For motifs with AND logic, GAMA achieves perfect retrieval at signal-to-noise ratios ≥80%.
GAMA shows significant correlation with binding affinities in synthetic antibody datasets.
In experimental antibody data, GAMA identifies key amino acid positions that partially overlap with known binding sites.
papers.limitation:
GAMA analyzes single positions within the sequence chain, limiting its ability to identify higher-order dependency patterns.
GAMA's capacity to discern motifs is constrained in environments with very low signal-to-noise ratios.
future_direction: Extending GAMA to identify higher-order dependency patterns
Applying GAMA to more complex datasets like Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire (AIRR) datasets
papers.abstract: Generative machine learning models offer a powerful framework for therapeutic design by efficiently exploring large spaces of biological sequences enriched for desirable properties. Unlike supervised learning methods, which require both positive and negative labeled data, generative models such as LSTMs can be trained solely on positively labeled sequences, for example, high-affinity antibodies. This is particularly advantageous in biological settings where negative data are scarce, unreliable, or biologically ill-defined. However, the lack of attribution methods for generative models has hindered the ability to extract interpretable biological insights from such models. To address this gap, we developed Generative Attribution Metric Analysis (GAMA), an attribution method for autoregressive generative models based on Integrated Gradients. We assessed GAMA using synthetic datasets with known ground truths to characterize its statistical behavior and validate its ability to recover biologically relevant features. We further demonstrated the utility of GAMA by applying it to experimental antibody-antigen binding data. GAMA enables model interpretability and the validation of generative sequence design strategies without the need for negative training data.

papers.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of Large Language Models (LLMs) to structural interventions like layer deletion and swapping, and can this inform a framework for depth-dependent computations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a four-stage framework (detokenization, feature engineering, prediction ensembling, residual sharpening) for interpreting depth-dependent computations in LLMs, based on behavioral and mechanistic evidence from layer-wise interventions.
papers.conclusion: This work introduces a four-stage framework for understanding inference in LLMs, which emerges across architectures and scales, suggesting transformers perform inference as an ordered composition of specialized computational regimes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are remarkably robust to layer deletion and swapping, retaining 72–95% of original top-1 accuracy without fine-tuning.
Performance degradation is not uniform: early and final layers are most sensitive, while middle layers are robust to interventions.
The pattern of sensitivity and other analyses motivate a hypothesis of four universal stages of inference observed across model families and sizes.
Evidence for each stage includes: early layers exhibit local attention and subjoiner heads (detokenization); middle layers show peak probing accuracy for semantic features (feature engineering); later layers show prediction and suppression neurons (ensembling and sharpening).
The residual architecture enables redundancy and self-repair, explaining the model's robustness to local interventions.
papers.limitation: Stage boundaries are approximate, and multiple stages may co-occur within a single layer. The framework reflects aggregate trends, whereas individual tokens may follow distinct processing paths.
future_direction: Future work can sharpen the stage boundaries.
Future work can link the stages to optimization dynamics.
Future work can provide a more theoretical framework.
papers.abstract: We investigate the robustness of Large Language Models (LLMs) to structural interventions by deleting and swapping adjacent layers during inference. Surprisingly, models retain 72-95% of their original top-1 prediction accuracy without any fine-tuning. We find that performance degradation is not uniform across layers: interventions to the early and final layers cause the most degradation, while the model is remarkably robust to dropping middle layers. This pattern of localized sensitivity motivates our hypothesis of four stages of inference, observed across diverse model families and sizes: (1) detokenization, where local context is integrated to lift raw token embeddings into higher-level representations; (2) feature engineering, where task- and entity-specific features are iteratively refined; (3) prediction ensembling, where hidden states are aggregated into plausible next-token predictions; and (4) residual sharpening, where irrelevant features are suppressed to finalize the output distribution. Synthesizing behavioral and mechanistic evidence, we provide a framework for interpreting depth-dependent computations in LLMs.

papers.title: Efficiently Quantifying and Mitigating Ripple Effects in Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently quantify and mitigate the ripple effect in the hidden space during model editing of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Graphical Impact Evaluation (GIE) to efficiently quantify the ripple effect in hidden space during model editing, and Selective Impact Revision (SIR) to mitigate this effect, demonstrating their effectiveness over existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods, GIE and SIR, effectively identify and alleviate the ripple effect in hidden space, contributing to more reliable and stable model editing techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The ripple effect in hidden space is a significant issue in all current model editing methods.
GIE detects 90% of the overall ripple effect with only 10% of the computational cost compared to a vanilla evaluation method.
SIR reduces the ripple effect intensity by 54.75% compared to the state-of-the-art model editing method.
The ripple effect differs based on the quantity and distribution of edits, with BFS-distributed edits causing more pronounced effects than random ones.
Excessive edits lead to model deterioration, as seen with methods like ROME and MEND when the number of edits exceeds 50.
papers.limitation: Due to the limitation of computation resources, experiments are performed on GPT2-XL rather than larger models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have revolutionized numerous tasks with their remarkable efficacy. However, editing these models, crucial for rectifying outdated or erroneous information, often leads to a complex issue known as the ripple effect in the hidden space. While difficult to detect, this effect can significantly impede the efficacy of model editing tasks and deteriorate model performance. This paper addresses this scientific challenge by proposing a novel evaluation methodology, Graphical Impact Evaluation(GIE), which quantitatively evaluates the adaptations of the model and the subsequent impact of editing. Furthermore, we introduce the Selective Impact Revision(SIR), a model editing method designed to mitigate this ripple effect. Our comprehensive evaluations reveal that the ripple effect in the hidden space is a significant issue in all current model editing methods. However, our proposed methods, GIE and SIR, effectively identify and alleviate this issue, contributing to the advancement of LLM editing techniques.

papers.title: Consistency of Feature Attribution in Deep Learning Architectures for Multi-Omics
papers.research_question: How consistent and robust is SHAP for feature attribution in multi-view deep learning models applied to multi-omics data, and how do architectural choices and randomness affect it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that SHAP feature rankings in multi-view deep learning models for multi-omics data are sensitive to architectural choices and random initialization, and proposes inspecting variation across runs to assess robustness.
papers.conclusion: SHAP shows great variability in feature importance rankings for multi-view deep learning models on multi-omics data, and researchers should use multiple training runs to inspect variation when identifying important biomolecules.
papers.key_findings:
SHAP rankings are sensitive to the addition of noise features and layer size choices, with correlation degrading as noise increases.
Variation in feature ranks across training runs due to random weight initialization is significant, with top-ranked features sometimes flipping to low ranks.
Dynamic layer sizing can stabilize SHAP values but may degrade model performance, while fixed layers show inconsistent effects depending on size.
Features selected by SHAP maintain discriminative power in downstream random forest classification, but clustering performance remains poor.
The consistency of SHAP rankings is not reliable, suggesting caution when using it for biomarker identification in multi-omics deep learning.
future_direction: Inspect the biological plausibility of features selected through visual inspection of variation in scores across runs.
Investigate reliable methods for remedying the observed variation in SHAP values.
papers.abstract: Machine and deep learning have grown in popularity and use in biological research over the last decade but still present challenges in interpretability of the fitted model. The development and use of metrics to determine features driving predictions and increase model interpretability continues to be an open area of research. We investigate the use of Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) on a multi-view deep learning model applied to multi-omics data for the purposes of identifying biomolecules of interest. Rankings of features via these attribution methods are compared across various architectures to evaluate consistency of the method. We perform multiple computational experiments to assess the robustness of SHAP and investigate modeling approaches and diagnostics to increase and measure the reliability of the identification of important features. Accuracy of a random-forest model fit on subsets of features selected as being most influential as well as clustering quality using only these features are used as a measure of effectiveness of the attribution method. Our findings indicate that the rankings of features resulting from SHAP are sensitive to the choice of architecture as well as different random initializations of weights, suggesting caution when using attribution methods on multi-view deep learning models applied to multi-omics data. We present an alternative, simple method to assess the robustness of identification of important biomolecules.

papers.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders extract relatively monosemantic features that are more interpretable than neurons, with most features being human-understandable.
Features can be used to intervene on and steer transformer generation, such as activating specific features to produce corresponding text like base64 or Arabic script.
Features are universal across different models and autoencoder runs, more similar to each other than to neurons, suggesting they reflect underlying data properties.
Features split into families as autoencoder size increases, providing different resolutions of understanding the same model components.
Despite having only 512 neurons, the MLP layer can represent tens of thousands of features through superposition, as shown by scaling the autoencoder.
papers.abstract: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition? Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis. Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.

papers.title: The Compositional Architecture of Regret in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which transformer layers’ hidden states most cleanly isolate the regret signal, and how is this signal represented with these layers?
papers.core_contribution: This work contributes valuable insights for neuron-level identification and provides methodological tools for analyzing similar cognitive states, advancing our understanding of how cognitive states are coded within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: This work advances our understanding of how cognitive states like regret are coded within LLMs through neuron-level identification and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Identified the optimal regret representation layer using the S-CDI metric, enhancing probe classification performance.
Discovered an M-shaped decoupling pattern across transformer layers, indicating alternating coupling and decoupling phases in information processing.
Categorized neurons into three functional groups (regret, non-regret, dual) using the RDS metric.
Showed that simultaneous intervention with regret and dual neurons substantially reduces regret classification performance, revealing a compositional architecture of regret at the neuron level.
Revealed that regret processing capabilities exhibit non-monotonic scaling across model sizes, with the 70B model showing superior performance.
papers.limitation: The non-monotonic scaling observed lacks more detailed investigation.
future_direction: Validation of the two-factor performance hypothesis in future work.
papers.abstract: Regret in Large Language Models refers to their explicit regret expression when presented with evidence contradicting their previously generated misinformation. Studying the regret mechanism is crucial for enhancing model reliability and helps in revealing how cognition is coded in neural networks. To understand this mechanism, we need to first identify regret expressions in model outputs, then analyze their internal representation. This analysis requires examining the model's hidden states, where information processing occurs at the neuron level. However, this faces three key challenges: (1) the absence of specialized datasets capturing regret expressions, (2) the lack of metrics to find the optimal regret representation layer, and (3) the lack of metrics for identifying and analyzing regret neurons. Addressing these limitations, we propose: (1) a workflow for constructing a comprehensive regret dataset through strategically designed prompting scenarios, (2) the Supervised Compression-Decoupling Index (S-CDI) metric to identify optimal regret representation layers, and (3) the Regret Dominance Score (RDS) metric to identify regret neurons and the Group Impact Coefficient (GIC) to analyze activation patterns. Our experimental results successfully identified the optimal regret representation layer using the S-CDI metric, which significantly enhanced performance in probe classification experiments. Additionally, we discovered an M-shaped decoupling pattern across model layers, revealing how information processing alternates between coupling and decoupling phases. Through the RDS metric, we categorized neurons into three distinct functional groups: regret neurons, non-regret neurons, and dual neurons.

papers.title: Compact Proofs of Model Performance via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to derive compact formal guarantees on model performance? Does more compact proof require and provide more mechanistic understanding, and does more faithful understanding lead to tighter bounds?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact formal proofs of model performance, and shows that more compact proofs require more mechanistic understanding and that more faithful understanding leads to tighter bounds.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact proofs of model performance, but compounding structureless errors pose a challenge that future work must address.
papers.key_findings:
Shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding.
More faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds.
Compounding structureless errors is a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.
papers.limitation:
Compounding structureless errors pose a challenge for generating compact proofs.
The approach is demonstrated only on a simple toy setting (Max-of-K).
future_direction: Addressing the challenge of compounding structureless errors in generating compact proofs.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We propose using mechanistic interpretability -- techniques for reverse engineering model weights into human-interpretable algorithms -- to derive and compactly prove formal guarantees on model performance. We prototype this approach by formally proving accuracy lower bounds for a small transformer trained on Max-of-K, validating proof transferability across 151 random seeds and four values of K. We create 102 different computer-assisted proof strategies and assess their length and tightness of bound on each of our models. Using quantitative metrics, we find that shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding. Moreover, we find that more faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds. We confirm these connections by qualitatively examining a subset of our proofs. Finally, we identify compounding structureless errors as a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.

papers.title: Breaking Bad Tokens: Detoxification of LLMs Using Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used to detoxify large language models through activation steering, and what are the trade-offs between toxicity reduction and model fluency?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first comprehensive evaluation of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for detoxifying large language models, introducing a three-tiered steering approach that enables precise toxicity reduction while preserving model capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based causal interventions show promise for LLM detoxification but have limitations such as fluency degradation in some models and feature splitting issues, suggesting practical guidelines for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based steering significantly reduces toxicity, especially at higher steering strengths, outperforming existing baselines by up to 20%.
There is a trade-off between toxicity reduction and fluency: stronger steering degrades fluency in GPT-2 Small but not in Gemma-2-2B.
Model capabilities (general NLP benchmark scores) remain stable after steering, indicating preservation of knowledge and general abilities.
Feature splitting in wider SAEs hampers safety interventions, but a simple composition-based approach can mitigate this effect.
Conditional steering (per-input and per-token) can preserve fluency better than constant steering, with per-token steering being less effective for detoxification in some cases.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models and toxicity, not covering multilingual or multimodal settings.
Reliance on automatic toxicity detectors (Detoxify) that may reflect biases in their training data and annotators.
Manual SAE feature selection is labor-intensive and may overlook context-dependent forms of toxicity.
Results are on specific model layers (layers 5 and 10 for GPT-2, 10 and 20 for Gemma) and may not generalize to other layers.
future_direction: Extend to multilingual and multimodal models to assess generalizability.
Use diverse data sources with human annotation to capture nuanced or culture-specific harms.
Develop scalable and robust approaches for SAE feature identification.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Encode Scientific Quality? An Empirical Study Using Monosemantic Features from Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concept of scientific quality using monosemantic features extracted from sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first systematic investigation into how LLMs encode scientific quality using monosemantic features from sparse autoencoders, identifying four key types of features related to research methodologies, publication types, high-impact fields, and scientific jargon.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode a rich and multidimensional representation of scientific quality through monosemantic features, capturing aspects like research methodologies, publication types, high-impact fields, and scientific jargon, providing insights into their internal mechanisms for research evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode features reflecting research methodologies, associating higher quality with rigorous methodological approaches.
Features related to publication type, such as survey papers and literature reviews, are associated with higher scholarly impact.
Features associated with high-impact research fields and technologies act as strong signals of perceived research importance.
Features corresponding to specific scientific jargons and academic language are identified, though their precise role is unclear.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of monosemantic features inherently involves a qualitative component, as semantic labels are assigned by human researchers and may introduce subjectivity.
This work focused exclusively on Gemma 2 models, limiting the generality of the results to other architectures.
The study classified publications into research quality quartiles rather than using regression to predict specific values.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other LLM architectures to assess the generality of the results.
Using regression to predict specific quality values instead of classification into quartiles.
Investigating how interpretable features can enhance LLM performance in tasks such as research evaluation, academic text generation, and hypothesis discovery.
papers.abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing use of generative AI, and large language models (LLMs) in particular, to support both the assessment and generation of scientific work. Although some studies have shown that LLMs can, to a certain extent, evaluate research according to perceived quality, our understanding of the internal mechanisms that enable this capability remains limited. This paper presents the first study that investigates how LLMs encode the concept of scientific quality through relevant monosemantic features extracted using sparse autoencoders. We derive such features under different experimental settings and assess their ability to serve as predictors across three tasks related to research quality: predicting citation count, journal SJR, and journal h-index. The results indicate that LLMs encode features associated with multiple dimensions of scientific quality. In particular, we identify four recurring types of features that capture key aspects of how research quality is represented: 1) features reflecting research methodologies; 2) features related to publication type, with literature reviews typically exhibiting higher impact; 3) features associated with high-impact research fields and technologies; and 4) features corresponding to specific scientific jargons. These findings represent an important step toward understanding how LLMs encapsulate concepts related to research quality.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Network Models for Toxicity Prediction by Extracting Learned Chemical Features
papers.research_question: How can neural network models for toxicity prediction be interpreted by extracting learned chemical features from hidden layers?
papers.core_contribution: A novel method to interpret neural network predictions for toxicity by extracting chemical substructures from hidden neurons, validated on mutagenicity data and shown to be competitive with established attribution methods.
papers.conclusion: The study presents a novel method to extract learned chemical information from hidden layers of neural networks and use these to explain model predictions, complementing more established techniques for understanding neural network models for toxicity prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The activation of hidden neurons in a neural network trained for toxicity prediction can be linked to specific chemical substructures (toxicophores).
The proposed method can extract substructures that correspond to known toxicophores for mutagenicity.
The explanations provided by the method (IG_hidden) are competitive with and complementary to those from input feature attribution (IG_input).
The method works well for single-layer networks but for deeper layers, neurons tend to aggregate multiple features and become less specific.
papers.limitation:
One neuron may be activated by a range of diverse chemical substructures, making it impossible to assign a single cause to the activation of a particular neuron.
Relevant chemical features may activate a large number of different neurons across the network, making interpretation complex.
It could be that none of the identified substructures associated with a highly activated neuron match the test compound.
future_direction: Extending the approach to regression models.
Using more generic representations of substructures such as SMARTS.
Applying the method to other toxicity endpoints and datasets.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have become a popular machine-learning technique for the toxicity prediction of chemicals. However, due to their complex structure, it is difficult to understand predictions made by these models which limits confidence. Current techniques to tackle this problem such as SHAP or integrated gradients provide insights by attributing importance to the input features of individual compounds. While these methods have produced promising results in some cases, they do not shed light on how representations of compounds are transformed in hidden layers, which constitute how neural networks learn. We present a novel technique to interpret neural networks which identifies chemical substructures in training data found to be responsible for the activation of hidden neurons. For individual test compounds, the importance of hidden neurons is determined, and the associated substructures are leveraged to explain the model prediction. Using structural alerts for mutagenicity from the Derek Nexus expert system as ground truth, we demonstrate the validity of the approach and show that model explanations are competitive with and complementary to explanations obtained from an established feature attribution method.

papers.title: Enhancing Neural Network Interpretability with Feature-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the feature learning of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to better align with input features, thereby enhancing their usefulness for neural network interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Mutual Feature Regularization (MFR), a regularization technique that trains multiple Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) in parallel with weight reinitialization and an auxiliary penalty to encourage learning similar features, leading to better alignment with input features and improved SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: MFR encourages SAEs to learn more features of the input, thereby increasing their usefulness for neural network interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MFR increases the correlation between feature similarity across SAEs and similarity with input features, as demonstrated on synthetic data.
On synthetic data, SAEs trained with MFR recover more of the known input features compared to baseline SAEs.
MFR improves reconstruction loss and loss recovered when training SAEs on GPT-2 Small MLP layer activations, with up to a 21.21% reduction in reconstruction loss.
MFR also improves reconstruction loss on EEG denoising tasks, though the benefits are smaller than for neural network activations.
The method involves conditionally reinitializing SAE weights based on inactive feature detection and adding an auxiliary penalty to encourage feature similarity across SAEs.
papers.limitation: MFR increases computational cost as it requires training multiple SAEs in parallel, which may become unmanageable for very large models.
future_direction: Investigate efficient mutual learning-based approaches for SAEs that can benefit from the positive relationship between feature similarity across SAEs and feature similarity with input features without requiring more compute.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in improving the interpretability of neural network activations, but can learn features that are not features of the input, limiting their effectiveness. We propose \textsc{Mutual Feature Regularization} \textbf{(MFR)}, a regularization technique for improving feature learning by encouraging SAEs trained in parallel to learn similar features. We motivate \textsc{MFR} by showing that features learned by multiple SAEs are more likely to correlate with features of the input. By training on synthetic data with known features of the input, we show that \textsc{MFR} can help SAEs learn those features, as we can directly compare the features learned by the SAE with the input features for the synthetic data. We then scale \textsc{MFR} to SAEs that are trained to denoise electroencephalography (EEG) data and SAEs that are trained to reconstruct GPT-2 Small activations. We show that \textsc{MFR} can improve the reconstruction loss of SAEs by up to 21.21\% on GPT-2 Small, and 6.67\% on EEG data. Our results suggest that the similarity between features learned by different SAEs can be leveraged to improve SAE training, thereby enhancing performance and the usefulness of SAEs for model interpretability.

papers.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the amortisation gap in sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and can more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that sparse autoencoder (SAE) encoders are inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference due to an amortisation gap, and demonstrates empirically that more expressive encoders (like MLPs) and sparse coding methods can outperform SAEs, leading to more interpretable features in large language models.
papers.conclusion: More sophisticated sparse inference methods, such as MLPs and sparse coding, can outperform traditional SAE encoders, reducing the amortisation gap and improving interpretability, which opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAE encoders have a provable amortisation gap, making them suboptimal for sparse inference even in solvable cases.
Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and sparse coding consistently outperform SAEs in recovering sparse codes, with sparse coding achieving the highest performance.
The performance advantage of more sophisticated methods is more pronounced in regimes where compressed sensing theory predicts recoverability.
These findings generalize to real-world applications, as shown by training on GPT-2 activations where MLPs yield more interpretable features than SAEs.
The amortisation gap can be reduced with increased compute, with MLPs surpassing SAE performance after a consistent computational threshold.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result on SAE suboptimality is proven for a specific setting (linear-nonlinear encoder, sparse signals in union of subspaces) and may not cover all practical SAE implementations.
future_direction: Pitting optimised sparse coding approaches (e.g., Least Angle Regression, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) against optimised SAE architectures.
Further exploration of top-k sparse coding with proper hyperparameter tuning to achieve Pareto improvements.
Scaling the methods to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work has shown promise in using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable features in neural network representations. However, the simple linear-nonlinear encoding mechanism in SAEs limits their ability to perform accurate sparse inference. Using compressed sensing theory, we prove that an SAE encoder is inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference, even in solvable cases. We then decouple encoding and decoding processes to empirically explore conditions where more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders. Our results reveal substantial performance gains with minimal compute increases in correct inference of sparse codes. We demonstrate this generalises to SAEs applied to large language models, where more expressive encoders achieve greater interpretability. This work opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations and analysing large language model activations.

papers.title: A Holistic Approach to Unifying Automatic Concept Extraction and Concept Importance Estimation
papers.research_question: How can we unify concept extraction and concept importance estimation in explainable AI, and how can we identify clusters of data points that share similar classification strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unifying framework for concept-based explainability that formalizes concept extraction as dictionary learning and concept importance as attribution, providing theoretical guarantees and new evaluation metrics.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential benefits of the dictionary learning framework for automatic concept extraction and hopes it will pave the way for further advancements in the field of XAI.
papers.key_findings:
NMF strikes a balance between PCA and K-Means for concept extraction, offering good reconstruction, sparsity, stability, and in-distribution reconstructions.
The last layer is preferable for both concept extraction and concept importance estimation.
For concept importance in the penultimate layer, Gradient Input, Integrated Gradients, Occlusion, and RISE are optimal for faithfulness metrics (C-Deletion, C-Insertion, C-µFidelity).
The strategic cluster graph visualizes the main classification strategies used by a model and helps explain misclassifications.
The framework enables the derivation of new concept importance methods and their evaluation using adapted faithfulness metrics.
papers.abstract: In recent years, concept-based approaches have emerged as some of the most promising explainability methods to help us interpret the decisions of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). These methods seek to discover intelligible visual 'concepts' buried within the complex patterns of ANN activations in two key steps: (1) concept extraction followed by (2) importance estimation. While these two steps are shared across methods, they all differ in their specific implementations. Here, we introduce a unifying theoretical framework that comprehensively defines and clarifies these two steps. This framework offers several advantages as it allows us: (i) to propose new evaluation metrics for comparing different concept extraction approaches; (ii) to leverage modern attribution methods and evaluation metrics to extend and systematically evaluate state-of-the-art concept-based approaches and importance estimation techniques; (iii) to derive theoretical guarantees regarding the optimality of such methods. We further leverage our framework to try to tackle a crucial question in explainability: how to efficiently identify clusters of data points that are classified based on a similar shared strategy. To illustrate these findings and to highlight the main strategies of a model, we introduce a visual representation called the strategic cluster graph. Finally, we present https://serre-lab.github.io/Lens, a dedicated website that offers a complete compilation of these visualizations for all classes of the ImageNet dataset.

papers.title: ENNGene: an Easy Neural Network model building tool for Genomics
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents ENNGene, a user-friendly tool with a graphical interface that simplifies the process of building, training, and interpreting deep learning models for genomics data.
papers.conclusion: ENNGene empowers genomics researchers to use deep learning for their data and will be an important tool for the genomics research community.
papers.key_findings:
ENNGene models achieve state-of-the-art performance on the RBP24 dataset, with an average AUROC of 0.947.
Including evolutionary conservation as an input branch improves performance for most proteins in the RBP24 dataset.
The tool provides interpretability through Integrated Gradients, highlighting important input positions.
papers.limitation: The tool currently requires manual tuning of hyperparameters and architecture selection, which could be automated in the future.
future_direction: Incorporating Neural Architecture Search (NAS) for automatic architecture optimization.
Adding a module for automated hyperparameter tuning.
Setting up a dedicated server with common genome references to simplify data input.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The recent big data revolution in Genomics, coupled with the emergence of Deep Learning as a set of powerful machine learning methods, has shifted the standard practices of machine learning for Genomics. Even though Deep Learning methods such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are becoming widespread in Genomics, developing and training such models is outside the ability of most researchers in the field. Results Here we present ENNGene - Easy Neural Network model building tool for Genomics. This tool simplifies training of custom CNN or hybrid CNN-RNN models on genomic data via an easy-to-use Graphical User Interface. ENNGene allows multiple input branches, including sequence, evolutionary conservation, and secondary structure, and performs all the necessary preprocessing steps, allowing simple input such as genomic coordinates. The network architecture is selected and fully customized by the user, from the number and types of the layers to each layer's precise set-up. ENNGene then deals with all steps of training and evaluation of the model, exporting valuable metrics such as multi-class ROC and precision-recall curve plots or TensorBoard log files. To facilitate interpretation of the predicted results, we deploy Integrated Gradients, providing the user with a graphical representation of an attribution level of each input position. To showcase the usage of ENNGene, we train multiple models on the RBP24 dataset, quickly reaching the state of the art while improving the performance on more than half of the proteins by including the evolutionary conservation score and tuning the network per protein. Conclusions As the role of DL in big data analysis in the near future is indisputable, it is important to make it available for a broader range of researchers. We believe that an easy-to-use tool such as ENNGene can allow Genomics researchers without a background in Computational Sciences to harness the power of DL to gain better insights into and extract important information from the large amounts of data available in the field. Contact panagiotis.alexiou@ceitec.muni.cz

papers.title: From Parameters to Performance: A Data-Driven Study on LLM Structure and Development
papers.research_question: How do structural configurations of large language models (LLMs) affect their performance across different benchmarks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a large-scale dataset of LLM structural configurations and performance, and provides data-driven insights into how specific structural parameters (like layer depth and FFN size) affect performance across different task types, validated through mechanistic interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: Structural parameters of LLMs have distinct and quantifiable impacts on different task types, and data-driven analysis combined with mechanistic interpretability can provide actionable insights for model optimization and design.
papers.key_findings:
Layer depth is the most influential structural factor for reasoning tasks (ARC-C, HellaSwag, WinoGrande).
FFN intermediate size (d_ffn) is the most important factor for knowledge- and math-oriented tasks (TruthfulQA, GSM8K).
Performance on ARC-C, HellaSwag, and WinoGrande is highly correlated, suggesting a shared reliance on reasoning ability.
MMLU is the most indicative benchmark for predicting a model's structural configuration.
Pruning layers with low Block Influence scores significantly degrades performance on reasoning tasks but has minimal effect on knowledge-focused tasks.
papers.limitation: The dataset may be biased towards certain model families (e.g., LLaMA) due to their overrepresentation in the open-source community.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across various domains, driving significant technological advancements and innovations. Despite the rapid growth in model scale and capability, systematic, data-driven research on how structural configurations affect performance remains scarce. To address this gap, we present a large-scale dataset encompassing diverse open-source LLM structures and their performance across multiple benchmarks. Leveraging this dataset, we conduct a systematic, data mining-driven analysis to validate and quantify the relationship between structural configurations and performance. Our study begins with a review of the historical development of LLMs and an exploration of potential future trends. We then analyze how various structural choices impact performance across benchmarks and further corroborate our findings using mechanistic interpretability techniques. By providing data-driven insights into LLM optimization, our work aims to guide the targeted development and application of future models. We will release our dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/DX0369/LLM-Structure-Performance-Dataset

papers.title: Interpretable LLM Guardrails via Sparse Representation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior to mitigate harmful, misleading, or biased content using sparse representation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SRS, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to disentangle activations into monosemantic features and steer LLM behavior via sparse steering vectors, achieving fine-grained control while preserving output quality.
papers.conclusion: SRS enables precise and interpretable steering of LLM behavior using sparse representations, providing a reliable guardrail for safety, fairness, and truthfulness with superior performance over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRS outperforms existing steering methods like CAA and SAE-TS in single-attribute and multi-attribute control tasks.
SRS maintains high linguistic quality, including grammatical correctness and language diversity, with minimal side effects.
SRS demonstrates robustness against diverse jailbreak prompts, achieving high defense rates.
Multi-attribute control with PCA composition strategy yields the best trade-off between control effectiveness and content quality.
Sparse features enable interpretable identification of attribute-relevant dimensions through KL divergence analysis.
papers.limitation: Multi-attribute steering strategies such as PCA may not fully capture complex relationships and conflicts between attributes.
future_direction: Layer-wise or component-wise multi-attribute steering to align interventions with semantic levels.
Context-aware and personalized steering based on semantic subdomains of prompts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities in generation tasks but are prone to producing harmful, misleading, or biased content, posing significant ethical and safety concerns. To mitigate such risks, representation engineering, which steer model behavior toward desired attributes by injecting carefully designed steering vectors into LLM's representations at inference time, has emerged as a promising alternative to fine-tuning approaches. However, due to the semantically entangled nature of LLM's representation, existing representation engineering methods still suffer from several limitations: limited fine-grained controllability, content quality degradation, and conflict in multi-attribute control. To overcome these challenges, we propose Sparse Representation Steering (SRS), a novel framework that achieves fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior by first disentangling internal activations into a sparse, semantically meaningful representation space, and then selectively steering relevant dimensions. Specifically, SRS leverages a pretrained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to transform dense, entangled activation patterns into a sparse monosemantic feature space. To identify relevant features, SRS contrasts sparse activations from positive and negative prompt pairs and measures their bidirectional KL divergence to locate dimensions most associated with the target attribute. We conduct comprehensive experiments on Gemma-2 series model across three alignment dimensions, i.e., safety, fairness, and truthfulness, to evaluate the effectiveness of SRS. Results show that SRS consistently outperforms existing steering methods, which achieves significantly improved controllability across both single and multiple attribute settings, while preserving high linguistic quality and general ability.

papers.title: CREME: Robustness Enhancement of Code LLMs via Layer-Aware Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of Code LLMs to natural language prompt perturbations via targeted, lightweight parameter updates (model editing)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CREME, a lightweight model editing framework that uses a single pair of original and perturbed prompts to identify robustness-sensitive layers via causal tracing and performs targeted parameter updates to align representations, enhancing model robustness to prompt perturbations.
